## Brake Noise + Wet-Stopping Check for a 2017 Toyota Corolla

Your symptoms point most strongly to **brake pad wear or glazed/contaminated pads**, with **rotor wear** as the next most likely factor. The wet-weather stopping change also makes it worth checking **tire tread and brake fluid condition**, not just the brakes themselves.

## Most Likely Causes, Ranked

| Likelihood | Possible cause | Why it fits | Typical repair range |
|---|---|---|---|
| High | **Worn brake pads** | Squeal at low speed is a classic wear indicator; 92,000 miles is a common replacement point | $150–$300 per axle |
| High | **Glazed pads or rotor surface rust/film** | Squeal can happen when pads get hard or the rotor surface is uneven | $150–$350 |
| Medium | **Rotors worn or uneven** | Longer stopping distance and noise can come from thin, grooved, or warped rotors | $250–$450 per axle |
| Medium | **Sticking caliper or slide pins** | Can cause uneven wear, heat, squeal, and reduced braking feel | $200–$450 |
| Medium | **Old brake fluid** | Can worsen pedal feel and braking performance, especially if moisture has built up | $90–$160 |
| Medium | **Tires with low tread or hard rubber** | Wet stopping distance is often tire-related, even when brakes are fine | $0–$600 depending on tire needs |
| Lower | **Brake hardware issue** | Missing anti-rattle clips, shims, or seized hardware can create squeal | $50–$150 added to brake job |

## Likely-Cause Checklist for a Mechanic

- **Pads:** Measure remaining pad thickness front and rear; ask if wear indicators are contacting the rotor.
- **Rotors:** Check rotor thickness, scoring, rust lip, and runout; ask whether resurfacing is safe or if replacement is better.
- **Calipers:** Confirm both front calipers slide freely and are not sticking.
- **Hardware:** Inspect shims, clips, and pad backing for missing or corroded parts.
- **Brake fluid:** Check fluid age and moisture contamination; ask when it was last flushed.
- **Tires:** Measure tread depth and look for uneven wear; ask whether wet stopping could be tire-limited rather than brake-limited.
- **Test drive:** Ask for a road test that reproduces the squeal at low speed and a straight-line stop on wet pavement if safe.

## Pads vs Rotors vs Something Else

| Symptom | More likely pads | More likely rotors | More likely something else |
|---|---|---|---|
| Squeal only at low speed | Yes | Sometimes | Yes, if hardware is loose |
| Grinding noise | No | Sometimes | Could be metal-on-metal wear |
| Steering wheel shake while braking | Sometimes | Yes | Less likely |
| Longer stopping in rain | Sometimes | Sometimes | **Very often tires** |
| Pedal feels soft or spongy | No | No | **Brake fluid or hydraulic issue** |
| Pulls to one side | Sometimes | Sometimes | **Caliper or alignment/tire issue** |

### What this means for your car
- If the pads are near the wear limit, a **full front brake service** is the most likely fix.
- If rotors are worn or glazed, expect **pads + rotors on the affected axle**.
- If the wet-weather issue is noticeable even when the brakes feel normal in dry conditions, **check tires before spending the full budget on brakes**.

## Repair Decision Guide Within $450

- **Best-case repair:** Front pads + hardware, and rotors reused if still within spec.
- **Common repair:** Front pads + rotors + hardware, likely near the top of your budget.
- **If rear brakes are also worn:** You may need to prioritize the axle with the worse wear first.
- **If tires are the real issue:** A brake repair alone may not fix wet stopping distance.

### Practical decision rule
- **Pads under 3 mm:** Replace pads now.
- **Rotors below spec, grooved, or warped:** Replace rotors with pads.
- **Uneven pad wear or hot smell after driving:** Check calipers/slide pins.
- **Pads and rotors look okay but wet stopping is poor:** Inspect tires and brake fluid next.

## Questions to Ask the Mechanic

- What is the **measured pad thickness** on each axle?
- Are the **rotors within minimum thickness spec**?
- Is there any **uneven wear** side-to-side or inner-to-outer pad difference?
- Are the **caliper slide pins moving freely**?
- Do the pads show **glazing, contamination, or cracking**?
- Are the **shims and anti-rattle clips** present and in good shape?
- Is the **brake fluid condition** acceptable, and when was it last flushed?
- How much of the wet stopping issue could be due to **tire tread depth**?
- Can you give me a **pad-only estimate** and a **pads + rotors estimate** before starting?

## Tension Headache Likely Triggers in Your Routine
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/thermometer-half.svg

Frequent headaches after long computer work are often linked to **muscle tension, posture strain, eye fatigue, stress load, sleep shortfall, and hydration/caffeine patterns**. With 6 weeks of recurring symptoms, it’s reasonable to focus on lifestyle contributors first while watching for warning signs.

## Practical Self-Care Plan for the Next 2 Weeks
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/clock.svg

- **Work breaks:** Stand up or reset posture every 30–45 minutes for 1–2 minutes.
- **Screen setup:** Keep the top of the monitor near eye level; avoid leaning your head forward.
- **Neck/shoulder release:** Do gentle neck rolls, shoulder shrugs, and upper-back stretches 2–3 times daily.
- **Hydration:** Aim for steady water intake through the day, especially if coffee replaces fluids.
- **Caffeine consistency:** Keep coffee timing and amount steady; avoid adding extra caffeine on headache days.
- **Sleep:** Try to move toward **7–8 hours** if possible, with a regular sleep/wake time.
- **Eye strain:** Use the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look 20 feet away for 20 seconds.
- **Pain relief:** If you usually tolerate them, occasional over-the-counter pain relievers can help, but avoid frequent use; using them too often can cause rebound headaches.

## When Headaches Need Medical Attention
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/exclamation-triangle.svg

Seek medical care if any of these happen:
- A **sudden, severe “worst headache”** or a headache that peaks rapidly
- New **weakness, numbness, confusion, fainting, trouble speaking, or vision loss**
- **Fever, stiff neck, rash**, or headache with significant illness
- Headache after a **head injury**
- Headaches that **wake you from sleep**, steadily worsen, or change in pattern
- **Persistent vomiting**
- New headaches with **jaw pain, scalp tenderness, or pain with chewing**
- Headaches becoming **more frequent or more intense** despite better sleep, breaks, and hydration
- Any headache pattern that feels clearly different from your usual tension-type headaches

Because your headaches have been frequent for **6 weeks**, it would also be reasonable to arrange a **non-urgent medical visit** if they continue, especially if they’re affecting work or need pain medicine often.

# 10-Day Data Analyst Interview Prep for Toronto

A focused plan for a mid-level role with **4 years’ experience**, strong **SQL/Excel**, basic **Python**, and a **retail analytics** background. The goal is to help you present as a business-minded analyst who can explain impact clearly and confidently discuss **CAD 85k–95k** compensation.

# 10-Day Prep Plan and Interview Focus

## 10-Day Prep Roadmap

| Day | Daily Tasks | Likely Interview Topics | Output by End of Day |
|---|---|---|---|
| Day 1 | Map your resume to the role; write a 60-second intro; list 6–8 projects | Career story, motivation, role fit | Tight personal pitch + target story bank |
| Day 2 | Review SQL joins, window functions, CTEs, aggregations; do 8–10 timed questions | SQL fundamentals, query logic, optimization | SQL refresh sheet + 3 strong examples |
| Day 3 | Practice Excel pivots, lookups, formulas, data cleaning shortcuts | Excel analysis, dashboarding, business reporting | Excel cheat sheet + one sample report story |
| Day 4 | Refresh Python basics: pandas, reading files, groupby, merge, missing values | Python for analysis, scripting, automation | 2 short Python walkthroughs you can explain |
| Day 5 | Build STAR stories for leadership, conflict, ambiguity, and impact | Behavioral questions, stakeholder management | 6 polished STAR stories |
| Day 6 | Translate retail analytics work into business outcomes; quantify impact | Metrics, experimentation, forecasting, retention | 3 impact stories with numbers |
| Day 7 | Practice case questions: root cause, KPI drop, dashboard request, segmentation | Case interview, problem solving, prioritization | Clear framework for handling cases |
| Day 8 | Mock interview round 1: 30 min technical + 30 min behavioral | Mixed interview format, communication | Notes on weak spots + improved answers |
| Day 9 | Compensation prep: salary range, negotiation script, Toronto market framing | Salary expectations, leveling, closing questions | Confident salary response + questions for interviewer |
| Day 10 | Full mock interview; review notes; refine intro, stories, and questions to ask | End-to-end interview readiness | Final interview packet and calm delivery |

## What to Emphasize in the Interview

- **Business impact first:** connect analysis to revenue, margin, conversion, retention, or operational efficiency.
- **Retail advantage:** your background is valuable because you understand customer behavior, store operations, inventory, promotions, and seasonal trends.
- **Mid-level readiness:** show you can work independently, clarify ambiguous problems, and influence stakeholders.
- **SQL + Excel strength:** position these as your core tools for fast, reliable analysis.
- **Python as a bonus:** frame it as useful for automation and deeper analysis, even if not your primary tool.

## 8 Practice Questions with Model Answer Outlines

### 1) Tell me about yourself.
- Start with your current role and years of experience.
- Mention retail analytics focus and the kinds of problems you solved.
- Highlight SQL, Excel, and basic Python.
- End with why you want this move and what value you bring.

### 2) Why are you moving from retail analytics to a broader data analyst role?
- Say you enjoyed turning data into business decisions.
- Explain you want a role with broader analytical scope and more cross-functional impact.
- Emphasize that retail gave you strong fundamentals in KPI analysis and stakeholder communication.
- Keep the tone positive, not like you are escaping retail.

### 3) Walk me through a SQL analysis you’ve done.
- State the business question first.
- Describe the tables, joins, filters, and aggregations used.
- Mention any window functions or CTEs if relevant.
- End with the business insight and action taken.

### 4) How do you handle messy or incomplete data?
- Explain your process: profile data, identify missingness, check consistency, define rules.
- Distinguish between fixing, imputing, excluding, or flagging data.
- Mention documenting assumptions.
- Give a real example if possible.

### 5) Describe a time you influenced a stakeholder with data.
- Use STAR format.
- Show how you adjusted your message for the audience.
- Explain how you linked analysis to a decision.
- End with measurable impact or adoption.

### 6) A dashboard KPI suddenly drops. What do you do?
- First validate the metric and data pipeline.
- Check time period, filters, definitions, and source changes.
- Break the issue into segments: channel, region, product, customer cohort.
- Conclude with root cause, recommendation, and next monitoring step.

### 7) How do you prioritize when multiple teams need analysis at once?
- Mention urgency, business impact, effort, and dependencies.
- Clarify deadlines and decision dates.
- Communicate trade-offs early.
- Show that you can balance speed with quality.

### 8) What salary are you looking for?
- Anchor to the market and your experience level.
- State a range such as **CAD 85,000–95,000**.
- Add that you’re flexible depending on scope, total compensation, and growth.
- Keep it confident and concise.

# Berlin Apartment Rental Checklist for 2026-08-01 Move-In

## Key Points to Review Before Signing
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/building.svg

- **Move-in date:** Confirm the lease start date is **2026-08-01** and that handover, keys, and condition protocol are aligned with it.
- **Deposit:** A **3-month deposit** is a common review point in Germany; check whether the amount is capped, how it is payable, and when it must be returned.
- **Repairs clause:** A clause making the tenant pay for **all repairs under 100 euros** deserves careful review, especially if it is broad or automatic.
- **Utilities and service charges:** Verify what is included in the rent, what is billed separately, and how annual reconciliation works.
- **Condition report:** Make sure the apartment handover protocol lists existing damage, meter readings, and missing items.
- **House rules:** Review rules on subletting, pets, quiet hours, renovations, and use of shared spaces.

## Questions to Ask the Landlord
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/phone.svg

- Is the **deposit held in a separate tenant deposit account**?
- Can the **deposit be paid in installments** rather than all at once?
- What exactly counts as a **repair under 100 euros**?
- Does the repair clause apply to **labor, parts, or both**?
- Are **wear-and-tear repairs** excluded from tenant payment?
- Who handles **appliance maintenance** and emergency repairs?
- Are there any **indexation, renewal, or termination** clauses that change the rent or notice period?
- Will the landlord provide a **signed handover protocol** on move-in day?

## Clauses That Deserve Extra Scrutiny
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/exclamation-triangle.svg

- **Repair cost clauses:** Especially if they shift routine maintenance to the tenant in a broad way.
- **Deposit terms:** Amount, payment timing, holding method, and refund timeline.
- **Operating cost clauses:** Anything that expands what the tenant must pay beyond standard service charges.
- **Renewal and termination clauses:** Notice periods, automatic extensions, and early exit terms.
- **Renovation or cosmetic obligations:** Painting, flooring, or “return to original condition” language.
- **Penalty or flat-fee clauses:** Any fixed costs for keys, cleaning, or damage that may be disproportionate.

## Compact Review Checklist
| Item | What to Check | Why It Matters |
|---|---|---|
| Lease dates | Start date, handover date, key transfer | Avoids move-in disputes |
| Deposit | Amount, payment schedule, separate account | Protects cash flow and refund rights |
| Repairs clause | Threshold, scope, exclusions | Prevents unfair routine-cost shifting |
| Rent breakdown | Cold rent, utilities, service charges | Clarifies total monthly cost |
| Condition report | Damage, meter readings, photos | Helps avoid later damage claims |
| Termination | Notice period, break options | Affects flexibility if plans change |
| House rules | Pets, noise, subletting, alterations | Prevents rule violations |

## Practical Takeaway
- The **deposit** and **repairs-under-100-euro** clause are the two biggest items to examine closely.
- Ask for any unclear term to be written in plain language before signing.
- If a clause seems unusually broad or one-sided, it is worth getting a local tenant association or lawyer to review it.

## Manchester 2-Bed Internet Setup Plan for 2026-09

A 78 m² apartment with one full-time WFH user fits best with a reliable mid-tier fibre plan, a Wi‑Fi 6 router, and simple mesh-ready placement. Budget-wise, **£40–£55/month** should comfortably cover a strong consumer package in Manchester.

## Recommended Setup by Priority

| Area | Recommended choice | Why it fits | Target spec |
|---|---|---|---|
| Connection speed | **150–300 Mbps down / 20–50 Mbps up** | Enough for video calls, streaming, cloud backups, and multiple devices without overspending | Fibre-to-the-premises if available |
| Router class | **Wi‑Fi 6 dual-band router** | Best balance of price, coverage, and stability for a 2-bed flat | 802.11ax, gigabit ports |
| Coverage approach | **Single router first, mesh-ready later** | 78 m² is often fine with one well-placed router; mesh only if walls are dense or signal drops | Add 1 node only if needed |
| Work-from-home priority | **Stable upload + low latency** | More important than very high download speed for calls and remote work | Prioritize latency and upload |
| Budget fit | **Mid-range fibre package** | Leaves room for a better router if the ISP bundle is weak | Around £40–£55/month total |

## Ideal Router Features and Placement

### Router features to look for
- **Wi‑Fi 6 (802.11ax)** for better multi-device performance
- **Dual-band** as the minimum; tri-band only if you later add mesh
- **Gigabit WAN/LAN ports** for fast fibre and wired work devices
- **Good QoS / device prioritization** for video calls and work laptop traffic
- **IPv6 support** and easy app-based management
- **Guest network** for visitors and smart-home isolation
- **At least 2 external antennas or strong internal antenna design** for apartment coverage

### Placement tips
- Put the router **near the center of the apartment**, not in a corner.
- Keep it **elevated and unobstructed**: on a shelf or cabinet, not on the floor.
- Avoid placing it **behind a TV, inside a cupboard, or next to metal appliances**.
- If your WFH desk is in one room, try to place the router where the **line of sight** to that room is best.
- If the apartment has thick walls or long corridors, plan for **mesh later** rather than buying an oversized single router now.
- Use **Ethernet** for the work laptop if possible; it is the simplest way to improve call stability.

### Connection speed guidance
- **Minimum workable:** 100 Mbps down / 10–20 Mbps up
- **Best value for your use:** 150–300 Mbps down / 20–50 Mbps up
- **Only worth paying more for if needed:** 500 Mbps+
  This is usually unnecessary for one WFH user unless you do large cloud uploads, frequent backups, or heavy shared streaming.

## Installation Day Checklist

- Confirm the **fibre type** and whether an **ONT** is included or already installed.
- Test the router in the **best central location first** before drilling or mounting anything.
- Change the **Wi‑Fi name and password** immediately.
- Set the **5 GHz network** for your laptop and TV/streaming devices.
- Keep a **2.4 GHz network** available for smart devices and longer-range coverage.
- Run a **speed test near the work desk** and again in the far bedroom.
- Check **video call quality** on Teams/Zoom/Meet for at least 10 minutes.
- Save your ISP login details, router admin password, and support number.
- If performance is weak, move the router once before deciding on mesh.
- If you use a desktop or docking station, connect it by **Ethernet** on day one.

## Best-Fit Recommendation

For your apartment and budget, the sweet spot is:

- **Plan:** 150–300 Mbps fibre
- **Router:** Wi‑Fi 6 dual-band, gigabit ports, QoS
- **Setup:** central placement, wired WFH device if possible
- **Upgrade path:** add a mesh node only if bedroom coverage is weak

This gives you stable work calls, good whole-flat coverage, and enough headroom without paying for speed you likely won’t use.

# Seasonal Allergy Relief Options

Mild seasonal allergy symptoms for 2 weeks, with no fever or breathing trouble, are often managed with non-drowsy over-the-counter measures. The goal is to reduce sneezing, itchy eyes, and a runny nose while staying alert at work.

## Common OTC Approaches for Daytime and Evening

Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/sun.svg

- **Non-drowsy oral antihistamines**: often used for sneezing, itchy eyes, and a runny nose.
  - Common examples: **cetirizine**, **loratadine**, **fexofenadine**
  - Best fit for office hours: usually less sedating than older antihistamines
  - Note: cetirizine can still make some people sleepy

- **Steroid nasal sprays**: helpful when symptoms last more than a few days or affect the nose most.
  - Common examples: **fluticasone**, **triamcinolone**, **mometasone**
  - Best for: congestion, runny nose, and overall nasal inflammation
  - Tip: these work best when used consistently for several days

- **Saline nasal rinse or spray**: can wash out pollen and thin mucus.
  - Best for: stuffiness, post-nasal drip, and irritation
  - Good option: morning and after coming indoors

- **Eye drops for allergies**: useful if itchy eyes are a main symptom.
  - Look for: **antihistamine eye drops** or **lubricating artificial tears**
  - Tip: artificial tears can help rinse allergens from the eyes

- **Avoiding triggers**: often improves symptoms without adding medication.
  - Shower or wash face after outdoor exposure
  - Keep windows closed during high-pollen times
  - Use a HEPA filter if available
  - Change clothes after being outside

## When Allergy Symptoms Need Medical Care

Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/phone.svg

Seek medical care promptly if any of these happen:
- **Breathing trouble, wheezing, chest tightness, or lip/tongue swelling**
- **Fever**, facial pain, or thick discolored nasal drainage that suggests infection
- **Symptoms lasting more than 2–4 weeks** despite OTC treatment
- **Severe eye redness, eye pain, light sensitivity, or vision changes**
- **One-sided facial pain or worsening sinus pressure**
- **Symptoms that interfere with sleep, work, or daily life**
- **Repeated need for OTC medicine without good relief**

Because the symptoms are already lasting 2 weeks, it is reasonable to try a structured OTC plan now and monitor whether improvement happens over the next 1–2 weeks.

## Morning and Evening Symptom Tracker

Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/calendar.svg

| Time | What to Record | Rating |
|---|---|---|
| Morning | Sneezing count, eye itch, runny nose, congestion, sleep quality | 0–3 each |
| Evening | Outdoor exposure, meds taken, symptom change, side effects, overall comfort | 0–3 each |

Simple scoring:
- **0** = none
- **1** = mild
- **2** = moderate
- **3** = severe

Helpful notes to add:
- Pollen exposure
- Time spent outdoors
- Any drowsiness from medication
- Whether symptoms improved after saline rinse or eye drops

## Practical Next Step

A common non-drowsy starting approach is:
- **One non-drowsy oral antihistamine in the morning**
- **Saline rinse or spray daily**
- **Add a steroid nasal spray** if nasal symptoms continue
- **Use allergy eye drops** if itchy eyes are prominent

If symptoms are not clearly better after a short trial, or if any warning signs appear, a clinician can help confirm allergies and rule out sinus infection or other causes.

## Sources

- American Academy of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology: https://www.aaaai.org/tools-for-the-public/conditions-library/allergies/allergic-rhinitis
- Mayo Clinic: https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/hay-fever/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20373040
- NHS: https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/hay-fever/

# Berlin Kitchen Sink Repair Checklist

A good fit here is a **weekday evening, English-speaking plumber** who can inspect and repair a leaking kitchen sink within **48 hours** and keep the total under **€180** if possible.

# What to Ask Before Booking

- Can you come **within 48 hours** and work **weekdays between 18:00 and 21:00**?
- Do you **speak English**?
- Can you provide an **itemized quote** before starting work?
- Is the price **all-in** or are **call-out, labor, parts, and VAT** separate?
- What is your **minimum charge** and **hourly rate**?
- Will you inspect for a leak at the **trap, faucet, supply lines, sealant, or drain connection**?
- If parts are needed, do you carry common parts or will you need a second visit?
- What is the **estimated total range** for a small apartment sink leak?
- Do you guarantee the repair, and for how long?
- Can you confirm **payment methods** and whether an invoice is provided?
- Can you send the quote by **email or WhatsApp** before the appointment?
- Are there any extra fees for **evening service** or **Berlin travel time**?

# Message Template to Send to Service Providers

Hello,

I need a plumber for a **leaking kitchen sink** in a **52 m² apartment in Berlin**.
I need service **within 48 hours**, preferably on a **weekday between 18:00 and 21:00**.

Please confirm:
- Whether you **speak English**
- Your **availability**
- An **itemized quote**
- Whether the total can stay **within €180**
- Any call-out fee, labor rate, parts cost, and VAT
- Whether you can bring common parts if needed

Please also let me know the likely cause of the leak and whether a single visit is enough.

Thank you.

## How to Choose Fast

- Prefer the quote with the **lowest all-in total** that is still **itemized**
- Reject any quote that does not clearly separate **labor, call-out, parts, and VAT**
- If two quotes are close, choose the one that confirms:

## Mid-Level PM Interview Prep for Dublin

You have a strong base for a mid-level PM move: SaaS domain experience, stakeholder strength, and enough SQL to handle product analytics conversations. Since you’re transitioning from operations and have 6 hours/week, the plan below focuses on the highest-yield interview skills for Dublin roles in your target salary band of **€75,000–€90,000**.

## 5-Week Product Manager Study Plan

| Week | Focus | Key Sessions | Goal |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | PM interview foundations | Product role framing; PM frameworks; Dublin market expectations; salary calibration | Build a clear “why PM, why now” story |
| 2 | Product sense | Product design prompts; customer problem framing; prioritization; trade-offs | Answer product sense questions with structure |
| 3 | Metrics and SQL | North Star metrics; funnel analysis; cohort basics; SQL practice on retention/conversion | Speak confidently about metrics and impact |
| 4 | Behavioral questions | STAR stories; conflict, influence, ambiguity, failure; ops-to-PM transition narrative | Prepare 6–8 reusable stories |
| 5 | Portfolio story outline + mock interviews | 1 flagship case study; tightening answers; mock interviews; compensation practice | Walk into interviews with a polished narrative |

## Weekly Breakdown for 6 Hours

### Week 1: PM Foundations
- 2h: Learn the PM interview loop and common question types
- 2h: Write your “Why PM / Why this company / Why Dublin” pitch
- 2h: Research 8–10 target companies and note product types, customers, and business models

### Week 2: Product Sense
- 2h: Practice problem framing using “who, what, why now”
- 2h: Work through 3 product design prompts out loud
- 2h: Review prioritization methods: RICE, impact vs effort, and trade-offs

### Week 3: Metrics + SQL
- 2h: Define metrics for SaaS products: activation, conversion, retention, churn, expansion
- 2h: Practice 3 SQL patterns: joins, group by, funnel analysis
- 2h: Explain how you’d diagnose a metric drop and what actions you’d take

### Week 4: Behavioral Stories
- 2h: Draft STAR stories for leadership, conflict, influence, ambiguity, and failure
- 2h: Convert ops experience into PM language: process improvement, customer pain, cross-functional impact
- 2h: Practice concise delivery: 90 seconds for short answers, 2–3 minutes for deeper stories

### Ranking rubric for listings

| Criterion | Weight | What to look for | Strong signal |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Transit commute to downtown | 30% | Door-to-door by bus/rail, not just driving time | 25 min or less during weekday commute hours |

# Ontario Freelance Design Business Checklist

A simple sole proprietorship in Ontario is usually straightforward to set up, but the main compliance work is in taxes, contracts, and recordkeeping. Since you’re working from home with one contractor and expect about **CAD 48,000** in annual revenue, the key question is whether you need to register for **GST/HST** and how you document business expenses and contractor payments.

## Main Registration and Setup Steps

- **Choose and confirm the business name**
  - If you operate under your own legal name, registration may not be required for the name itself.
  - If you use a different business name, register it in Ontario.

- **Register the sole proprietorship**
  - Register the business name with Ontario if needed.
  - Get a **Business Number (BN)** from the CRA if you need tax program accounts.

- **Decide on GST/HST registration**
  - With expected revenue of **CAD 48,000**, you are above the small supplier threshold of **CAD 30,000** in taxable supplies over four consecutive calendar quarters.
  - That usually means you should register for GST/HST and charge it on taxable work, unless a specific exception applies.

- **Set up a business bank account**
  - Not always legally required, but strongly recommended for clean bookkeeping and audit trail.

- **Check local home-based business rules**
  - Review any municipal zoning, condo, lease, or home insurance restrictions that may affect working from home.

- **Register for payroll only if needed**
  - If the contractor is truly an independent contractor, payroll registration is usually not needed.
  - If the relationship looks like employment, payroll obligations can change quickly.

## Tax and Invoicing Considerations

| Topic | Practical point | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Income tax | Sole proprietors report business income on their personal return | Track all income and deductible expenses during the year |
| GST/HST | Likely required at your revenue level | Register, charge tax on taxable invoices, and file returns on time |
| Invoicing | Invoices should support tax and bookkeeping | Include your business name, date, invoice number, client details, services, fees, and GST/HST if registered |
| Home office | You may be able to claim a reasonable portion of home expenses | Keep square footage and expense records for the workspace calculation |
| Contractor payments | Contractor fees are generally deductible if legitimate business expenses | Keep contracts, invoices, and proof of payment |
| Instalments | May apply if tax owing becomes significant | Review CRA instalment requirements after your first year or two |

### Invoicing details to include
- Your legal name or business name
- Business address or mailing address
- Client name and address
- Unique invoice number
- Date of issue
- Description of design services
- Rate, quantity, subtotal
- GST/HST amount and registration number, if registered
- Payment due date and payment method

## Common Contract Clauses to Include

- **Scope of work**
  - Define deliverables, revisions, file formats, and what is excluded.

- **Fees and payment terms**
  - State hourly rate, project fee, deposit, milestones, late fees, and currency.

- **Change requests**
  - Explain how extra work is approved and billed.

- **Timeline and client responsibilities**
  - Set deadlines for feedback, approvals, and materials the client must provide.

- **Intellectual property**
  - Clarify when ownership transfers, what happens before full payment, and whether you retain portfolio rights.

- **Confidentiality**
  - Protect client information and any unreleased concepts.

- **Termination**
  - State how either party can end the project and how partial work is paid.

- **Independent contractor status**
  - Make clear the contractor relationship is not employment if that is the true arrangement.

- **Liability limitation**
  - Consider a reasonable cap on damages and exclusion of indirect losses.

- **Dispute resolution**
  - Include governing law, venue, and a simple escalation process.

## Records to Keep for Compliance

- Client contracts and signed proposals
- Invoices issued and invoices received
- Proof of payment, such as bank statements or receipts
- Expense receipts for software, equipment, subscriptions, advertising, and supplies
- Home office records, including workspace measurements and utility calculations
- GST/HST records, including amounts charged and remitted
- Contractor agreements and contractor invoices
- Project correspondence showing approvals, scope changes, and deliverables
- Mileage or travel logs, if any business travel occurs
- Asset purchase records for equipment and software
- Copies of filed tax returns and supporting schedules
- Business registration documents and CRA correspondence

## Practical Compliance Notes

- Keep business and personal spending separate from day one.
- Save records in an organized digital folder system by year and category.
- Review contractor status carefully if you control their hours, tools, or work process.
- If you register for GST/HST, invoice consistently and remit collected tax on time.
- For a home office, only claim the business-use portion that is reasonable and supportable.

## 30-Day Headache Reduction Plan
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/clipboard2-pulse.svg

A practical, non-emergency routine for mild seasonal allergies plus occasional tension headaches. This plan focuses on sleep, hydration, posture, allergy control, and early symptom tracking.

## Daily Routine and 30-Day Action Plan
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/calendar-check.svg

| Timeframe | What to do | Why it helps |
|---|---|---|
| Morning | Drink water; eat breakfast; take a 5-minute neck/shoulder stretch; check pollen level and keep windows closed if high | Prevents dehydration, reduces muscle tension, limits allergy triggers |
| Midday | Take a 2–3 minute screen break every hour; relax jaw; keep shoulders down; have lunch on time | Reduces tension buildup and eye strain |
| Afternoon | If allergies flare, rinse face and change clothes after outdoor exposure; consider showering before bed | Lowers pollen exposure |
| Evening | Limit alcohol; reduce caffeine after early afternoon; do a 10-minute walk or light stretch; dim screens 1 hour before sleep | Supports sleep quality and headache prevention |
| Bedtime | Keep a consistent sleep schedule; use a cool, quiet room; try 5 slow breaths and a brief neck relaxation routine | Sleep regularity is one of the strongest headache protectors |

### 30-Day Progression
- **Days 1–7:** Start the routine, track headaches, and identify triggers.
- **Days 8–14:** Tighten sleep and screen habits; keep hydration steady.
- **Days 15–21:** Add stronger allergy control on high-pollen days; review posture and workstation setup.
- **Days 22–30:** Look for patterns in timing, food, sleep loss, stress, and pollen exposure; keep the most helpful habits.

### Simple prevention habits
- Aim for regular sleep and wake times, even on weekends.
- Drink enough fluids so urine is pale yellow most of the day.
- Keep meals regular; skipped meals can trigger headaches.
- Use a neutral neck position at your desk; raise screens to eye level.
- If allergies are active, reduce outdoor exposure during peak pollen hours when possible.
- Avoid overusing pain relievers, since frequent use can cause rebound headaches.

## When a Clinician Visit Is Important
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/exclamation-triangle.svg

| Warning sign | What it may mean | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Sudden, severe “worst headache” | Possible emergency cause | Seek urgent medical care now |
| Headache with fever, stiff neck, confusion, fainting, seizure, or rash | Possible infection or other serious condition | Get urgent evaluation |
| New weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, facial droop, or vision loss | Possible neurologic problem | Seek urgent medical care now |
| Headache after head injury | Concussion or bleeding risk | Get evaluated promptly |
| Headaches that are getting more frequent, more intense, or changing pattern | Needs medical review | Book a clinician visit |
| Headache with persistent vomiting or waking you from sleep repeatedly | Needs assessment | Book a clinician visit soon |
| Headache plus very high blood pressure symptoms, chest pain, or shortness of breath | Possible urgent issue | Seek urgent care |
| Headache that starts after age 50, or with cancer/immunosuppression history | Needs prompt review | Contact a clinician |

### Visit a clinician within 1–2 weeks if
- You are having headaches more than once a week.
- The headaches are interfering with work, sleep, or exercise.
- You suspect allergies are driving symptoms and over-the-counter measures are not enough.
- You want help choosing a safe allergy plan or headache treatment strategy.

# Toronto 2-Bedroom Lease Negotiation Checklist

For a **2-bedroom apartment in Toronto** at **CAD 2,850/month**, a **12-month lease**, and **move-in on 2026-06-01**, the main goals are to confirm the lease is lawful, reduce upfront cost where possible, and lock in any repair promises before signing.

## Lease Terms to Verify Before You Sign

- **Rent amount and inclusions**
  - Confirm the base rent is **CAD 2,850** and ask what is included: heat, water, hydro, internet, parking, locker, and laundry.
- **Lease start and possession**
  - Verify the lease start date matches **2026-06-01** and that you get keys, access fobs, and move-in instructions on day one.
- **Deposit terms**
  - In Ontario, landlords typically can ask for a **last month’s rent deposit** and a **key deposit** only, not a large damage/security deposit.
- **Rent increase timing**
  - Check whether the unit is rent-controlled and whether any increase would follow Ontario rules after the lease term.
- **Repairs and maintenance**
  - Make sure any promised repairs are written into the lease or a signed addendum, including timing and responsibility.
- **Utilities and services**
  - Clarify who pays each utility and whether any service interruptions or restrictions exist.
- **Assignment/sublet rights**
  - Confirm whether you may assign or sublet the unit and what approval process applies.
- **Early termination**
  - Ask whether there is a break-lease option, assignment option, or replacement tenant process.
- **Parking, pets, smoking, and guests**
  - Verify all building rules that could affect your use of the unit.
- **Condition report**
  - Request a move-in inspection checklist with photos before you accept possession.

## Questions to Ask the Landlord or Property Manager

| Topic | Question to Ask | Why It Matters |
|---|---|---|
| Deposits | What deposits are required beyond last month’s rent and key deposit? | Helps avoid unlawful or inflated upfront charges |
| Repairs | Can the needed repairs be completed before move-in, and can that be added in writing? | Protects you if the unit is not ready |
| Utilities | Which utilities are included in the rent, and which are billed separately? | Prevents surprise monthly costs |
| Rent control | Is this unit subject to Ontario rent-control rules? | Affects future rent increases |
| Move-in condition | Will you provide a signed condition report and photos at handover? | Helps protect your deposit and repair claims |
| Lease flexibility | Can the lease be assigned or sublet if my plans change? | Gives you an exit path |
| Access | How many keys/fobs are included, and what is the replacement fee? | Avoids extra move-in costs |
| Maintenance | What is the response time for urgent repairs and routine maintenance? | Sets expectations for service |

## Negotiation Points That Fit This Rental

- **Lower upfront deposit**
  - Ask to limit the deposit to **last month’s rent + key deposit only**.
- **Repair completion before move-in**
  - Request that all current issues be fixed before **2026-06-01**.
- **Rent concessions**
  - If repairs are delayed, ask for a **small rent credit** or a **free first week**.
- **Included services**
  - Negotiate for **parking**, **internet**, or **one utility** to be included if the rent is firm.
- **Lease clarity**
  - Ask for a written addendum confirming any promised work, appliance replacements, or cleaning.

## Winter Brake Noise + Fuel-Economy Drop: Priority Triage for Your 2016 Honda Civic

Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/car-front.svg

Your symptoms point to **two likely systems**: the **brakes** and an **engine/sensor/fueling issue**. The brake squeal is the most immediate safety item; the brief check-engine light and 10% MPG drop deserve prompt diagnosis, but they are usually less urgent unless the light returns or the car starts running rough.

## Prioritized Troubleshooting Plan

| Priority | Likely cause | What to check first | Urgency | Typical repair range |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Brake pads worn to wear indicator / glazed pads | Inspect pad thickness, rotor condition, and dust/debris in brakes | **Urgent** | **$150–$450 per axle** |
| 2 | Sticking caliper or slide pins | Check for uneven pad wear, hot wheel, pulling, dragging smell | **Urgent** if present | **$180–$700 per axle** |
| 3 | Brake hardware or rotor rust/glaze from winter use | Look for surface rust, lip on rotors, squeal only on light braking | **Soon** | **$80–$300** |
| 4 | Loose gas cap / EVAP fault / minor intermittent sensor issue | Scan stored codes, inspect cap seal, re-tighten or replace cap | **Soon** | **$20–$200** |
| 5 | Dirty air filter, aging spark plugs, or weak ignition coil | Check maintenance interval, misfire history, plug condition | **Soon** | **$60–$450** |
| 6 | Winter driving pattern causing lower MPG naturally | Short trips, cold starts, idling, winter fuel, tire pressure | **Monitor** | **$0–$80** |

## Most Likely Causes by Symptom

### Brake squeal
- **Most likely:** worn brake pads or pad wear indicators contacting the rotor
- **Also common in winter:** rust film on rotors after sitting, glazed pads, dirty caliper hardware
- **More concerning:** one caliper sticking, which can create heat, drag, and faster pad wear

### Check engine light came on once, then went off
- **Most likely:** intermittent EVAP issue, loose gas cap, or a sensor reading that cleared itself
- **Less likely but important:** a pending misfire, oxygen sensor, or fuel-trim issue that only appears under certain conditions
- **Key point:** even if the light is off now, the code may still be stored as a pending or history code

### Fuel economy dropped about 10%
- **Very plausible in winter city driving:** cold engine, idling, denser air, winter-blend fuel, shorter trips
- **Mechanical causes to rule out:** low tire pressure, dragging brakes, dirty air filter, spark plugs due, thermostat stuck open, sensor/fuel-trim issue

## Urgent vs Safe to Monitor

### Urgent now
- Brake squeal that is getting louder or happens on most stops
- Grinding, vibration, steering pull, or brake pedal pulsation
- Burning smell, one wheel much hotter than the others, or reduced braking performance
- Check engine light flashing or returning repeatedly

### Safe to monitor briefly
- A one-time check engine light that stayed off
- A modest MPG drop during winter city driving if the car otherwise runs smoothly
- Light squeal only on first morning stops if brakes still feel normal, though it should still be inspected soon

## Recommended Order of Action

1. **Inspect brakes first**
   - Measure pad thickness
   - Check rotor condition
   - Confirm calipers slide freely
   - Look for uneven wear or one wheel running hot

2. **Scan for codes now, even if the light is off**
   - Read stored and pending OBD-II codes
   - Note freeze-frame data if available
   - Clear only after recording the code

3. **Check simple MPG-loss causes**
   - Tire pressure, especially in winter
   - Air filter condition
   - Any dragging brake after a short drive
   - Fuel cap seal and EVAP hose condition

4. **If no brake issue is found, move to engine tune-up items**
   - Spark plugs
   - Air filter
   - Throttle body cleanliness
   - Fuel trims and O2 sensor data

## Cost Priorities

- **Lowest-cost first checks:** tire pressure, gas cap, OBD scan, visual brake inspection
- **Common repair range:** **$150–$450** if it is mainly pads/rotors
- **If caliper or hardware is involved:** often **$250–$700+**
- **If the MPG issue is sensor/tune-up related:** usually **$60–$450**, depending on parts needed

# College Laptop Buying Rubric for a $900 Budget

A good match for your workload is a **thin-and-light 14-inch laptop** with **16 GB RAM**, **512 GB SSD**, and a **modern efficient CPU**. ## Recommended Spec Priority Order

1. **Battery life and efficiency**
   - Target: **8+ hours real-world use**
   - Look for efficient CPUs like Intel Core Ultra, AMD Ryzen U-series, or Apple M-series
   - Avoid power-hungry gaming chips unless you need them

2. **Display quality**
   - Target: **14-inch**, 1080p or better
   - Prefer **IPS or OLED**, good brightness, and decent color accuracy
   - This matters a lot for reading, writing, and photo editing

3. **Memory**
   - Target: **16 GB RAM**
   - Helps with multitasking, browser tabs, spreadsheets, and editing
   - Prefer soldered 16 GB only if you are sure it is enough long-term

4. **Storage**
   - Target: **512 GB SSD**
   - Good baseline for school files, apps, and photos
   - 1 TB is nice, but not necessary inside your budget

5. **Weight and build**
   - Aim for **under 3.3 lb / 1.5 kg**
   - A sturdier chassis is worth paying for if you carry it daily

6. **Keyboard, trackpad, webcam**
   - Comfortable keyboard is important for long writing sessions
   - Webcam should be at least **1080p** if possible for calls

## Desk-Related Lower Back Pain: Quick Self-Care Plan

Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/thermometer-half.svg

A 34-year-old with 3 weeks of intermittent low back pain after long desk hours, without numbness, fever, or injury, most often fits a mechanical/overuse pattern. Since ibuprofen is not an option, this plan focuses on safe OTC choices, posture changes, and gradual movement.

## Safe Self-Care, Ergonomics, and 7-Day Activity Plan

### Safe self-care checklist
- **Keep moving:** short walks and gentle position changes every 30–45 minutes.
- **Use heat:** a warm pack or heating pad for 15–20 minutes at a time, several times daily.
- **Try acetaminophen if safe for you:** follow the package label; avoid if you have liver disease or heavy alcohol use.
- **Sleep support:** side-sleep with a pillow between knees, or on your back with a pillow under knees.
- **Avoid long bed rest:** normal light activity is usually better than staying still.
- **Avoid heavy lifting/twisting** for now, especially when pain is flared.
- **Consider topical options:** if you tolerate them, some people use topical analgesic creams or patches; follow label directions and avoid broken skin.

### Desk adjustments that usually help
- **Chair height:** feet flat on the floor, knees roughly level with hips.
- **Lumbar support:** use a small rolled towel or lumbar cushion at the small of the back.
- **Monitor height:** top of screen near eye level; screen centered in front of you.
- **Keyboard and mouse:** close enough that elbows stay near your sides.
- **Sitting time:** stand, stretch, or walk for 1–2 minutes every 30–45 minutes.
- **Task setup:** keep phone, notebook, and frequently used items within easy reach.
- **Posture cue:** aim for “supported upright,” not rigid straight-backed sitting.

### Warning signs that need medical attention
- **Numbness, tingling, or weakness** in a leg or foot
- **Pain shooting below the knee** that is worsening or persistent
- **Loss of bladder or bowel control**
- **Numbness in the groin or saddle area**
- **Fever, chills, unexplained weight loss, or feeling unwell**
- **Pain after a fall, accident, or other injury**
- **Severe pain that is constant, rapidly worsening, or wakes you from sleep**
- **Pain that is not improving after a few weeks** of self-care, or is limiting daily function

### 7-day activity plan
- **Day 1:** Heat + gentle walking
  - 10–15 minute easy walk, 2–3 times
  - Gentle back-friendly movement only; no heavy lifting
  - Set a timer for posture breaks every 30–45 minutes
- **Day 2:** Mobility day
  - Repeat walking
  - Add light stretches if comfortable: knees-to-chest only if it feels good, gentle hamstring stretch, pelvic tilts
  - Stop any movement that increases pain sharply
- **Day 3:** Desk reset day
  - Re-check chair, screen, and keyboard setup
  - Use lumbar support all day
  - Take one 2-minute standing break each hour at minimum
- **Day 4:** Build tolerance
  - 15–20 minute walk
  - Continue heat after work if sore
  - Avoid long uninterrupted sitting blocks
- **Day 5:** Core-friendly movement
  - Gentle bodyweight activities if comfortable: short wall sits, bird-dog style movements, or pelvic tilts
  - Keep reps low and pain-free
- **Day 6:** Normal activity day
  - Resume routine tasks with careful lifting technique
  - Bend at hips and knees, keep objects close to the body
- **Day 7:** Check progress
  - Compare pain, stiffness, and sitting tolerance to Day 1
  - If clearly improving, continue the same routine for another week
  - If not improving, or if symptoms change, arrange a medical visit

## Ontario Lease Change Snapshot

This looks like a **fixed-term Ontario residential tenancy** that started on **2025-09-01**. A rent increase on **2026-03-01** may be possible only if it follows Ontario rules, including proper notice and timing; the one-month deposit is usually treated as a **rent deposit**, not an extra fee.

## Tenant Checklist for Documents, Questions, and Reply

| Topic | What to keep or ask | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Lease paperwork | Signed lease, all addenda, renewal letters, move-in condition notes | Proves the agreed rent, term, and any special terms |
| Rent records | Receipts, e-transfers, bank statements, landlord messages | Shows what was paid and when |
| Deposit record | Proof of the one-month deposit and how the landlord described it | Helps confirm whether it was a lawful rent deposit |
| Rent increase notice | Copy of any written notice, date received, effective date | Lets you check whether notice and timing are proper |
| Building history | Ask whether the unit is rent-controlled and when it was first occupied for residential use | Helps determine whether annual guideline limits may apply |
| Repairs/issues | Photos, repair requests, response dates | Useful if the rent increase is being discussed alongside maintenance problems |

### Questions to ask the landlord
- Is this increase being treated as a formal Ontario rent increase notice?
- What is the current lawful rent, and what exact amount is being requested?
- When was the last rent increase, and what was the effective date?
- Is the unit subject to Ontario rent control based on first residential occupancy?
- Is the one-month deposit being held as a rent deposit, and will it be applied only to the last month of tenancy?
- Can you send the notice and supporting details in writing?

### Practical tenant checklist
- Keep everything in one folder: lease, notices, receipts, emails, texts, photos.
- Save screenshots of any messages with dates visible.
- Do not rely on verbal conversations alone.
- Compare the proposed increase date against the date of the last increase.
- If the notice seems improper, reply politely in writing and ask for clarification before paying more.
- If you need to challenge it later, your paper trail will matter more than phone calls.

### Polite written reply
Use a calm, non-accusatory tone:
- Confirm you received the message.
- Ask for the increase details in writing.
- State that you want to review the notice and lease terms.
- Do not admit the increase is valid if you are unsure.
- Keep the message short and professional.

## Sample Email Draft

Subject: Request for Written Details About Proposed Rent Increase

Hello [Landlord Name],

Thank you for your message about the proposed rent increase effective 2026-03-01.

I would appreciate it if you could send the increase details in writing, including the current lawful rent, the amount requested, the effective date, and the notice form or basis being relied on. I would also like to confirm how the one-month deposit is being held and whether the unit is subject to Ontario rent control.

I am reviewing the lease and my records, and I will respond once I have the written details.

Thank you,
[Tenant Name]

## Family Dinner Fit for Mexico City on Friday Night

A good choice here is a **casual taquería or Mexican fonda** with clear prices, easy customization, and mild options. For 4 people under **900 MXN total**, the best value usually comes from sharing tacos, quesadillas, aguas frescas, and one or two non-spicy mains.

| Child dislikes spicy food | Grilled, roasted, or cheese-based items; sauces on the side | Avoids heat and surprises | “Sin picante” is understood |
| Mexican/casual tacos | Tortillería or taquería with simple menu | Fast, kid-friendly, flexible | Tacos al pastor, suadero, bistec, quesadillas |

- **Optional child-safe extra**: plain quesadilla or tortilla with cheese

A practical spend target:
- Food: **650–780 MXN**
- Drinks: **80–160 MXN**
- Tip: **10–15%**, if service is seated and attentive

## Menu Check Before You Sit Down

- Look for **posted prices** and avoid places that only quote “market price”
- Confirm there are **at least 2 vegetarian choices**
- Ask whether sauces are **served separately**
- Check if kids can get **plain quesadillas, arroz, frijoles, or tortillas**
- Make sure the place can keep the bill low with **sharing-friendly portions**
- If the restaurant is seated service, ask whether **service is included** before tipping extra

## Tipping and Payment Checklist

- **Counter service / taquería casual:** small tip or rounding up is fine
- **Table service:** **10%** is a solid default; **15%** for very good service
- If service is already included, you can tip extra only if you want to
- Keep some **cash in MXN**, since smaller places may prefer it
- Ask for the bill early if you want to stay within budget and avoid over-ordering

# 7-Day Energy + Sleep Routine for a Busy Office Week

A realistic plan built around **4 short workouts**, **simple meals**, **steady energy**, and **better sleep**. It assumes you want low-friction cooking, repeatable groceries, and enough flexibility for office hours.

## Weekly Routine at a Glance

| Day | Exercise | Meals Focus | Sleep Focus |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mon | 35 min strength + walk | High-protein breakfast, easy lunch | Consistent bedtime, no late caffeine |
| Tue | 30 min brisk cardio | Simple leftovers, fruit snack | Wind-down routine, screens down early |
| Wed | Rest or light mobility | Balanced meals, steady hydration | Earlier dinner, calm evening |
| Thu | 35 min strength | Protein + carbs around workout | Keep dinner lighter |
| Fri | 30–40 min cardio or intervals | Easy prep meals, avoid heavy late snack | Aim for same sleep time |
| Sat | 40 min full-body circuit + walk | Flexible meals, one enjoyable meal | Relaxed but not too late |
| Sun | 20–30 min mobility + easy walk | Grocery prep day, simple batch cooking | Early reset for Monday |

## 7-Day Meal-and-Exercise Plan

### Day 1: Monday — Strong Start
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/thermometer-half.svg
- **Morning:** 10–15 min sunlight walk, then breakfast with protein.
- **Workout:** 35 min full-body strength: squats, push-ups, rows, glute bridges, planks.
- **Meals:** Oatmeal with banana and peanut butter; chicken/rice/veg bowl; eggs or yogurt at dinner if needed.
- **Snack:** Apple + peanut butter or Greek yogurt.
- **Hydration:** 2–2.5 L water; add a glass at breakfast and one mid-afternoon.
- **Sleep:** Stop caffeine by 2 PM; aim for a 30-minute wind-down.

### Day 2: Tuesday — Cardio + Light Eating
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/heart-pulse.svg
- **Morning:** Water first, then coffee/tea if you use it.
- **Workout:** 30 min brisk walk, bike, or easy jog.
- **Meals:** Eggs + toast; turkey or tuna sandwich; rice bowl with frozen vegetables.
- **Snack:** Carrots + hummus or a handful of nuts.
- **Hydration:** 2–3 L water, especially if allergies make you feel dry.
- **Sleep:** Keep dinner simple and finish 2–3 hours before bed.

### Day 3: Wednesday — Recovery Day
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/moon-stars.svg
- **Morning:** 5–10 min mobility or stretching.
- **Workout:** Rest day; optional 20-minute easy walk.
- **Meals:** Yogurt + oats + fruit; leftovers for lunch; pasta with chicken or beans for dinner.
- **Snack:** Banana or string cheese.
- **Hydration:** Keep a bottle at your desk and refill twice.
- **Sleep:** Lower lights in the evening; keep bedtime consistent.

### Day 4: Thursday — Strength + Protein
- **Morning:** Short walk or commute movement break.
- **Workout:** 35 min strength: lunges, overhead press, dead bug, hip hinge, side plank.
- **Meals:** Protein-forward breakfast; lunch with rice, chicken, and vegetables; dinner with salmon, tofu, or beans.
- **Snack:** Cottage cheese, yogurt, or nuts + fruit.
- **Hydration:** 2–2.5 L water; add electrolytes only if you sweat heavily.
- **Sleep:** Avoid a heavy dessert or alcohol close to bedtime.

### Day 5: Friday — Easy Cardio + Reset
- **Morning:** Light breakfast before work if you wake hungry.
- **Workout:** 30–40 min cardio, or 20 min cardio + 10 min mobility.
- **Meals:** Overnight oats or eggs; simple sandwich lunch; stir-fry or sheet-pan dinner.
- **Snack:** Fruit + nuts or hummus + crackers.
- **Hydration:** 1 glass on waking, 1 mid-morning, 1 mid-afternoon, 1 with dinner.
- **Sleep:** Try to keep the same bedtime as weekdays.

### Day 6: Saturday — Longer, Flexible Session
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/tree.svg
- **Morning:** Easy breakfast, then workout.
- **Workout:** 40 min full-body circuit: 5 moves, 3 rounds, moderate effort.
- **Meals:** Brunch-style eggs/toast/fruit; lunch leftovers; dinner can be your most enjoyable meal.
- **Snack:** Smoothie or yogurt if you’re active.
- **Hydration:** 2–3 L water; sip during the workout.
- **Sleep:** Keep late-night snacking moderate so sleep stays solid.

### Day 7: Sunday — Recovery + Prep
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/calendar-check.svg
- **Morning:** 20–30 min walk or yoga.
- **Workout:** Light mobility only.
- **Meals:** Batch-cook for the week: rice, roasted vegetables, chicken/beans, boiled eggs.
- **Snack:** Fruit, nuts, or yogurt.
- **Hydration:** Refill your water bottle and prep for Monday.
- **Sleep:** Go to bed a little earlier to reset the week.

## Simple Grocery Plan on $120/Month

This budget works best if you repeat a few affordable staples and cook in batches.

| Item | Weekly Use | Budget-Friendly Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Oats | Breakfast | Cheap, filling, good for energy |
| Eggs | Breakfast/dinner | Easy protein, quick to cook |
| Greek yogurt | Snack/breakfast | High protein, pairs with fruit |
| Rice | Lunch/dinner base | Batch-cook once, use all week |
| Chicken thighs or breast | Main protein | Buy in bulk when on sale |
| Canned tuna or beans | Backup protein | Great for fast lunches |
| Frozen vegetables | Lunch/dinner | Low waste, easy prep |
| Bananas/apples | Snacks | Portable office snacks |
| Peanut butter | Breakfast/snack | Cheap calories and staying power |
| Whole-grain bread or tortillas | Lunches | Fast sandwich or wrap option |

## Meal Templates You Can Repeat

- **Breakfast options**
  - Oatmeal + banana + peanut butter
  - Eggs + toast + fruit
  - Greek yogurt + oats + berries

- **Lunch options**
  - Chicken/rice/vegetable bowl
  - Tuna sandwich + fruit
  - Bean burrito wrap + yogurt

- **Dinner options**
  - Stir-fry rice bowl
  - Sheet-pan chicken and vegetables
  - Pasta with beans, spinach, and olive oil

- **Snack options**
  - Fruit + nuts
  - Yogurt
  - Hummus + carrots
  - Peanut butter toast

## Energy, Hydration, and Sleep Targets

- **Water:** Aim for **2–3 L/day**, more on workout days or during allergy season.
- **Caffeine:** Keep it earlier in the day; avoid it after **2 PM** if sleep is a goal.
- **Protein:** Try to include protein at **every meal** to reduce afternoon crashes.
- **Sleep:** Target a **consistent 7.5–8.5 hours** with the same bedtime most nights.
- **Allergies:** If symptoms are active, prioritize hydration, showering after outdoor exercise, and keeping workouts moderate rather than maximal.

# Electrician Hiring Checklist for a Madrid Apartment

For a **62 m² apartment in Madrid**, the safest approach is to hire a **licensed, insured electrician** who can confirm the scope, provide a written quote, and schedule the work within **2 weeks**. Your budget of **€250–€450** is reasonable for a small, mixed repair job if no major rewiring or panel replacement is needed.

## Vetting Checklist and Hiring Questions

### What to verify before booking
- **Licensed/qualified in Spain**: Ask for their professional registration or qualifying credentials for electrical work.
- **Insurance**: Confirm **civil liability insurance** covers accidental damage.
- **Written quote**: Request a line-by-line estimate for labor, materials, call-out, and VAT.
- **Scope fit**: Make sure they explicitly accept:
  - 8 outlet replacements
  - inspection of 2 ceiling lights
  - diagnosis and repair of 1 breaker issue
- **Availability**: Confirm they can complete the job **within 14 days**.
- **Materials policy**: Ask whether outlets/switches are included or supplied by you.
- **Warranty**: Ask for a short warranty on labor and parts.
- **References or reviews**: Prefer recent local reviews from Madrid or nearby neighborhoods.

### Questions to ask
- Are you **licensed/qualified** to do residential electrical work in Madrid?
- Do you have **liability insurance**?
- Can you provide a **written quote before starting**?
- Does your quote include **VAT, travel, and minor materials**?
- Will you **replace 8 outlets**, inspect **2 ceiling lights**, and diagnose the **breaker issue** in one visit?
- If you find a hidden issue, how do you handle **change orders**?
- What brand/type of outlets do you recommend for a standard apartment?
- How long will the work take, and how soon can you schedule it?
- Do you offer a **warranty** on the work?
- Will you provide an **invoice/receipt**?

### Red flags
- Refuses to give a written quote
- Won’t confirm insurance or credentials
- Says the breaker issue “must be fixed later” without inspection
- Quotes a very low price without seeing the job
- Pushes cash-only payment with no invoice

## Best Way to Structure the Job

| Item | What to request | What to confirm |
|---|---|---|
| Outlets | Replace 8 outlets | Same style/amp rating, safe installation, test each one |
| Ceiling lights | Inspect 2 fixtures | Wiring, mounting, switches, safe operation |
| Breaker issue | Diagnose and fix | Cause, parts needed, any safety risk |
| Timing | Complete within 2 weeks | Exact visit date and estimated duration |
| Budget | €250–€450 | Labor, materials, VAT, and any extras included |

Estoy buscando un electricista **autorizado/qualificado** para un trabajo en un apartamento de **62 m² en Madrid**. El trabajo no es urgente, pero me gustaría hacerlo **dentro de 2 semanas**.

Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/check2-square.svg

## Exchange-Rate Comparison for 2,000 USD

For a 2,000 USD conversion, **Service C** gives the highest euros received after fees.
The key tradeoff: **percentage fees** scale with the amount, while a **flat fee** hurts more on smaller transfers.

## Net Euros Received by Service

| Service | Gross EUR at Rate | Fee Type | Fee Amount | Net EUR Received |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|
| A | 2,000 × 0.91 = 1,820.00 | 1.5% | 30.00 USD equivalent | 1,792.70 |
| B | 2,000 × 0.92 = 1,840.00 | Flat | 12.00 USD | 1,828.96 |
| C | 2,000 × 0.905 = 1,810.00 | 0.8% | 16.00 USD equivalent | 1,795.12 |

## Math Breakdown

### Service A
- Gross conversion: 2,000 × 0.91 = **1,820.00 EUR**
- Fee: 1.5% of 2,000 = **30 USD**
- Fee converted at the same rate: 30 × 0.91 = **27.30 EUR**
- Net: 1,820.00 - 27.30 = **1,792.70 EUR**

### Service B
- Gross conversion: 2,000 × 0.92 = **1,840.00 EUR**
- Flat fee: **12 USD**
- Fee converted at the same rate: 12 × 0.92 = **11.04 EUR**
- Net: 1,840.00 - 11.04 = **1,828.96 EUR**

### Service C
- Gross conversion: 2,000 × 0.905 = **1,810.00 EUR**
- Fee: 0.8% of 2,000 = **16 USD**
- Fee converted at the same rate: 16 × 0.905 = **14.48 EUR**
- Net: 1,810.00 - 14.48 = **1,795.12 EUR**

## Best Choice

- **Best overall: Service B**
- It delivers the **most euros: 1,828.96 EUR**
- Even though it has a flat fee, its **better exchange rate (0.92)** outweighs the $12 charge for this amount

## Fee Tradeoff Insight

- **Percentage fee services**:
  - Better for smaller transfers if the rate is strong
  - Cost rises as the transfer amount rises
- **Flat fee services**:
  - Better for larger transfers because the fee stays fixed
  - Can be expensive on small transfers
- In this case, **Service B’s flat fee is small enough** that its superior exchange rate wins

## Budget Health Check

**Income left after core fixed costs:** $3,075
**After variable spending:** $2,555
**After $1,200 savings goal:** **$1,355 remaining**

This plan is **workable**, but it leaves several pressure points:
- **Groceries at $650** may be tight if the household has 3+ people or includes frequent takeout.
- **Transit at $220** can spike with fuel prices, repairs, or commuting changes.
- **Variable spending at $520** is the biggest category likely to drift upward.
- The **$355 buffer** is helpful, but not large enough to absorb multiple surprises in the same month.

## Overspending Risks to Watch

- **Food creep:** grocery runs plus takeout can push food costs well above plan.
- **Lifestyle leakage:** subscriptions, delivery fees, app purchases, and convenience spending add up fast.
- **Irregular transportation costs:** tires, oil changes, registration, and repairs are often missed.
- **Vacation fund conflict:** if travel is booked before the fund is fully built, savings can get raided.
- **Annual bills:** insurance renewals, gifts, school costs, and taxes can break a monthly plan if not reserved.

## 5 Cuts or Reallocations to Keep It Realistic

1. **Cap variable spending at $400 instead of $520**
   - Frees **$120/month**
   - Best for dining out, entertainment, and impulse purchases

2. **Trim subscriptions from $45 to $25**
   - Frees **$20/month**
   - Cancel or rotate one service at a time

3. **Reduce grocery spending from $650 to $600**
   - Frees **$50/month**
   - Use a meal plan, store brands, and one weekly shopping trip

4. **Move $100 from vacation fund to emergency fund for the first 6 months**
   - Improves short-term stability
   - Then restore vacation savings once the emergency cushion is stronger

5. **Split the $355 buffer into a “sinking fund”**
   - Put **$200** toward annual/irregular bills
   - Keep **$155** as true cash buffer
   - This prevents surprise expenses from disrupting savings

# 8-Week Headache and Sleep Reset

A practical, non-emergency plan built around your schedule: **3 x 30-minute workouts/week**, **no caffeine after 2 PM**, and simple daily habits to lower tension headaches and support better sleep.

## Weekly Wellness Plan

| Week | Focus | Exercise (3x/week, 30 min) | Daily Habit | Sleep Goal |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Baseline + consistency | Brisk walk, easy bike, light strength | Track headaches, sleep time, triggers | Fixed wake time daily |
| 2 | Posture + movement breaks | Walk + mobility; bodyweight circuit | 2–3 posture breaks during workday | Wind-down starts 45 min before bed |
| 3 | Hydration + regular meals | Moderate cardio + core | Drink steadily through morning/afternoon | Same bedtime 5 nights/week |
| 4 | Stress downshift | Cardio + stretching | 5-minute breathing reset daily | Reduce screen time before bed |
| 5 | Sleep environment | Strength + mobility | Dark, cool, quiet bedroom setup | Bed only for sleep/rest |
| 6 | Headache prevention | Cardio + neck/upper-back mobility | Check jaw/shoulder tension twice daily | Keep sleep/wake times steady |
| 7 | Fine-tune triggers | Mix of cardio and strength | Review food, stress, screen, and hydration patterns | Aim for faster sleep onset |
| 8 | Maintain what works | Favorite 3 workouts | Keep the most effective habits | Lock in a sustainable routine |

## Daily Routine for Headache Relief and Better Sleep

**Morning**
- Get **5–15 minutes of outdoor light** soon after waking.
- Drink a full glass of water.
- Do 2 minutes of neck, shoulder, and upper-back mobility.
- If you use caffeine, keep it earlier in the day and stop by **2 PM**.

**Workday**
- Use a **50/10 or 25/5** focus-break rhythm.
- Every hour, do 30–60 seconds of:
  - shoulder rolls
  - chin tucks
  - chest opener stretch
  - standing and looking far away to relax eye strain
- Keep screens at a comfortable height so your head does not drift forward.
- Eat regular meals; skipped meals can trigger headaches for some people.

**Evening**
- Finish exercise at least **2–3 hours before bed** if possible.
- Dim lights and reduce bright screens in the last **45–60 minutes**.
- Keep the room **cool, dark, and quiet**.
- Use a consistent wind-down: shower, reading, stretching, or calm music.

## Sleep Hygiene Checklist

- [ ] Wake up at the same time every day, including weekends
- [ ] Keep bedtime within about 1 hour most nights
- [ ] No caffeine after 2 PM
- [ ] Limit alcohol near bedtime
- [ ] Avoid large meals right before bed
- [ ] Keep naps short, ideally under 20–30 minutes and not late in the day
- [ ] Use the bed only for sleep and intimacy
- [ ] If you are awake for a long time, get up briefly and do something quiet
- [ ] Turn down lights and screens before bed
- [ ] Keep the bedroom cool and uncluttered

## Hydration, Meals, and Desk-Job Posture

### Hydration
- Aim for steady intake across the day rather than “catching up” at night.
- A simple target for many adults is **pale yellow urine** most of the day.
- Add water around workouts and on dry allergy days.
- If you get headaches from dehydration, keep a bottle at your desk and sip regularly.

### Desk posture
- Feet flat on the floor or on a footrest.
- Hips and knees roughly at 90 degrees.
- Screen top near eye level.
- Elbows near your sides; shoulders relaxed.
- Keyboard and mouse close enough that you do not reach forward.
- If you use a laptop, consider raising it and using an external keyboard/mouse.

### Quick tension-break sequence
- 5 slow shoulder rolls
- 5 chin tucks
- 20-second chest stretch
- 20-second upper-trap stretch each side
- 3 deep breaths with long exhales

## Exercise Plan for 3 Days a Week

**Day A: Cardio + mobility**
- 20 minutes brisk walking, cycling, or elliptical
- 10 minutes mobility: neck, shoulders, thoracic spine, hips

**Day B: Light strength**
- 2–3 rounds of:
  - squats or sit-to-stands
  - wall or incline push-ups
  - rows with band or light weights
  - glute bridges
  - dead bug or bird-dog
- Keep effort moderate, not exhausting

**Day C: Cardio + relaxation**
- 20 minutes moderate cardio
- 10 minutes stretching or yoga-style recovery

## When to See a Clinician

Make an appointment if any of these happen:
- Headaches become **more frequent, more severe, or change in pattern**
- Headaches wake you from sleep or are consistently worse in the morning
- You develop **vision changes, weakness, numbness, confusion, fainting, fever, or neck stiffness**
- Headaches start after a head injury
- Over-the-counter pain relief is needed often, or headaches persist despite good sleep and hydration
- Sleep problems last **more than 8 weeks** or cause major daytime impairment
- Loud snoring, gasping, or witnessed breathing pauses suggest possible sleep apnea
- Allergy symptoms are persistent enough to disrupt sleep, especially with congestion or mouth breathing

# 6-Month Spanish Path from A1 to B1

A steady **5 hours/week** can get you from beginner to solid intermediate if you keep the focus tight: **travel speaking, pronunciation, and high-frequency grammar**. This plan is built around short daily exposure, weekly speaking, and regular review so you keep moving without overload.

## Weekly Milestone Roadmap

| Week | Focus | Key sessions | Milestone |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sound system + greetings | Pronunciation app drills; basic phrases; 10-minute shadowing | Introduce yourself, greet, spell your name |
| 2 | Numbers, time, and travel basics | Podcast listening; airport/hotel vocabulary; mini speaking prompts | Ask for time, prices, and simple directions |
| 3 | Present tense: ser/estar/hay | Grammar app lesson; sentence building; speaking practice | Describe people, places, and what exists |
| 4 | Present tense: regular verbs | Daily verb drills; travel situations; short self-talk | Say what you do, need, want, and like |
| 5 | Articles, gender, plurals | Grammar review; vocab sorting; pronunciation cleanup | Make basic noun phrases correctly |
| 6 | Food and ordering | Restaurant dialogues; listening; role-play | Order food and ask about the menu |
| 7 | Question words + survival travel | Podcast + Q&A practice; speaking prompts | Ask where, when, how much, and how |
| 8 | Past intro: preterite of common verbs | Simple story practice; review deck; speaking | Describe what you did yesterday |
| 9 | Present continuous + routine talk | Listening; daily routine narration; pronunciation | Explain what you are doing now |
| 10 | Travel logistics | Booking, transport, check-in vocabulary | Handle buses, trains, hotels, and tickets |
| 11 | Direct object pronouns intro | Short grammar drills; substitution practice | Replace repeated nouns in simple sentences |
| 12 | Review + checkpoint | Mixed quiz; speaking recap; error review | Reach stable A1 and early A2 control |
| 13 | Reflexive verbs + daily life | App practice; speaking on routines; shadowing | Talk about getting ready, waking up, habits |
| 14 | Comparisons + preferences | Travel comparisons; opinion sentences | Compare places, food, and options |
| 15 | Imperfect intro for descriptions | Listening; story descriptions; guided speaking | Describe places and routines in the past |
| 16 | Pronunciation focus block | Stress, vowel clarity, linked speech | Improve clarity and reduce hesitation |
| 17 | Travel problem-solving | Missed train, wrong turn, hotel issue role-plays | Explain a problem and ask for help |
| 18 | Future with ir a + plans | Planning phrases; trip discussion | Say where you are going and why |
| 19 | Object pronouns + common connectors | Sentence expansion; conversation practice | Speak more naturally and avoid repetition |
| 20 | Listening stretch | Podcast summaries; slow native audio | Catch the main idea of short travel clips |
| 21 | B1 grammar consolidation | Mixed tense review; guided writing | Use present, preterite, imperfect with more control |
| 22 | Opinion and justification | Speaking on destinations, food, activities | Give simple reasons and preferences |
| 23 | Conversation endurance | 15-minute speaking sessions; follow-up questions | Keep a short conversation going |
| 24 | Final review and B1 readiness | Full review cycle; mock travel role-play | Manage common travel conversations with confidence |

## Weekly Study Structure and Review System

| Weekly block | Time | What to do | Best tool type |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Pronunciation | 45 min | Shadow 1 short audio, repeat tricky sounds, record yourself | App + podcast |
| Grammar | 75 min | Learn 1 small grammar point and make 10–15 sentences | App |
| Travel vocabulary | 45 min | Learn words in a real scenario: hotel, airport, restaurant, transport | App + flashcards |
| Listening | 60 min | Listen to a short podcast episode twice; note key phrases | Podcast |
| Speaking practice | 75 min | Self-talk, partner exchange, or tutor conversation | Speaking app / tutor |
| Review + test | 20 min | Spaced repetition, error log, quick recap quiz | Flashcards |

### Review system
- **Daily:** 10–15 minutes of spaced repetition for words, phrases, and example sentences.
- **Weekly:** Review the last 2 weeks before learning new material.
- **Monthly:** Do one speaking checkpoint and one mixed grammar/listening checkpoint.
- **Error log:** Keep a short list of recurring mistakes; review it every Friday.
- **Rule:** If you miss a week, do not skip ahead—use the next review block to catch up.

## Recommended Tool Mix

- **Apps:** Duolingo, Busuu, Babbel, or Memrise for structure and vocabulary.
- **Pronunciation:** Forvo, SpanishDict audio, and shadowing with slow native clips.
- **Podcasts:** Coffee Break Spanish, Notes in Spanish, or SpanishPod101 beginner lessons.
- **Speaking practice:** italki, Tandem, HelloTalk, or a language exchange partner.
- **Flashcards:** Anki or Quizlet for travel phrases and high-frequency grammar patterns.

## Berlin Lease Clauses in Plain English

These two clauses usually mean:

- **Rent increase tied to the local rent index**: the landlord may adjust your rent once a year, but the increase should be linked to the official local reference rent system for Berlin, not set arbitrarily.
- **Subletting only with written permission**: you cannot let someone else live there under your lease unless the landlord gives explicit written approval first.

## What to Check Before You Sign

| Clause | Plain-English meaning | What to confirm |
|---|---|---|
| Rent increase based on local rent index | Rent can go up, but only using the local benchmark | Which index is used, how often it can change, and how the increase is calculated |
| Once per year | The landlord should not raise rent more than once in a 12-month period | When the last increase was, and when the next one could legally start |
| Sublet only with written permission | You need approval before subletting any part of the apartment | Whether permission is for one person, one room, or any sublet at all |
| Written permission | Verbal approval is not enough | Who must sign it and how you should request it |

## Questions to Ask Before Signing

- Which exact rent index or reference system will be used for increases?
- How will I be notified of a rent increase, and how much notice will I get?
- Is there a cap on how much the rent can rise in one year?
- Does “sublet” include short-term guests, a roommate, or only a paying tenant?
- What is the process for requesting written permission to sublet?
- Can permission be refused for any reason, or only for specific reasons?
- Will the landlord’s approval be valid for future sublets, or only one person/time period?
- Can I keep a copy of all rent-increase notices and approvals in writing?

## Documents to Keep

- Signed lease and all addenda
- Any rent index explanation or calculation sheet
- All rent-increase notices
- Written sublet permission, if granted
- Email threads or letters about lease terms
- Move-in inspection report and photos
- Deposit receipt or proof of payment
- Proof of monthly rent payments
- Landlord contact details and property management contacts
- Any written promises made before signing

## Practical Takeaway

- The rent clause means **the landlord can raise rent, but not randomly**.
- The sublet clause means **get written approval before anyone else moves in or pays you rent**.
- The safest move is to keep **everything in writing** and save copies from day one.
