# GRE 10-Day Prep Plan for a Full-Time Schedule

A focused 10-day sprint can work well if you keep weekdays tight and use weekends for deeper practice. This plan prioritizes **quantitative reasoning, vocabulary, and writing**, with **one review day** and **one mock test day**, built around your available study time.

## 10-Day Study Schedule

| Day | Study Time | Focus | Daily Tasks | Goal |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| Day 1 | 1.5h | Quant foundations | 20 min formula refresh; 40 min timed arithmetic/algebra set; 30 min error review | Rebuild core math speed |
| Day 2 | 1.5h | Vocabulary | 45 min high-frequency GRE words; 30 min sentence usage; 15 min recall quiz | Start active word retention |
| Day 3 | 1.5h | Writing | 20 min issue-task structure; 40 min Issue essay outline + intro; 30 min analyze 2 sample essays | Lock in essay framework |
| Day 4 | 1.5h | Quant practice | 15 min warm-up; 45 min data interpretation/word problems; 30 min review mistakes | Improve accuracy under time |
| Day 5 | 1.5h | Vocabulary + writing | 30 min vocab drill; 45 min Argument essay outline + body plan; 15 min quick recall | Strengthen verbal expression |
| Day 6 | 4h, morning preferred | Deep quant + verbal | 90 min mixed quant set; 60 min vocab review; 45 min reading comprehension; 45 min error log cleanup | Build stamina on weekend time |
| Day 7 | 4h | Review day | 90 min review all missed quant questions; 60 min vocab consolidation; 60 min writing review; 30 min flashcard test | Fix weak spots before mock |
| Day 8 | 1.5h | Writing + quant reset | 40 min timed Issue essay; 35 min quant mini-set; 15 min review; 20 min vocab maintenance | Keep all sections active |
| Day 9 | 4h, morning preferred | Mock test day | 3h 45m full GRE mock under test conditions; 15 min break/reset notes | Simulate exam day |
| Day 10 | 1.5h | Post-mock review | 45 min analyze mock errors; 30 min redo missed questions; 15 min vocab refresh | Convert mistakes into gains |

## Daily Execution Plan

### Day 1: Quant Foundations
- Focus on arithmetic, fractions, ratios, and basic algebra.
- Keep an error log: write why each missed question was missed.
- End with 5-minute recall of formulas without notes.

### Day 2: Vocabulary
- Use a small, repeatable list of high-frequency GRE words.
- Practice each word in a sentence, not just definitions.
- Finish with a closed-book recall quiz.

### Day 3: Writing
- Build a reusable template for Issue essays.
- Practice one strong introduction and one clear thesis.
- Review sample essays to see what earns higher scores.

### Day 4: Quant Practice
- Work on data interpretation and word problems.
- Time yourself strictly to build pacing.
- Review every mistake immediately after the set.

### Day 5: Vocabulary + Writing
- Reinforce words you already saw earlier in the plan.
- Draft an Argument essay outline with evidence and counterpoint.
- Keep the session light but focused to avoid overload.

### Day 6: Weekend Deep Work
- Use the longer block for mixed practice.
- Start with quant while your energy is highest.
- End by cleaning up your notes and error log.

### Day 7: Review Day
- Revisit every missed or guessed question from Days 1–6.
- Group mistakes into patterns: careless, concept gap, timing, or misread.
- Re-test yourself on the same topics after review.

### Day 8: Writing + Quant Reset
- Write one timed Issue essay to maintain speed.
- Do a short quant set to keep your math sharp.
- Finish with quick vocab review, not new material.

### Day 9: Mock Test Day
- Take a full-length GRE mock in the morning if possible.
- Use official timing and minimal interruptions.
- Afterward, note only broad patterns; save deep review for Day 10.

### Day 10: Post-Mock Review
- Focus on the highest-value mistakes from the mock.
- Redo missed quant problems without looking at solutions first.
- Refresh vocab lightly so retention stays active.

# Weekly Wellness Routine for Screen Strain, Hydration, and Sleep

A simple routine can help reduce afternoon headaches, support allergy comfort, and improve sleep without pushing your monthly budget. This plan stays non-emergency and uses low-cost habits first, with a few optional OTC items to discuss with a pharmacist.

## Practical Weekly Plan

| Day/Time | Focus | Habit | Goal |
|---|---|---|---|
| Daily morning | Start hydrated | Drink 12–16 oz water within 30 minutes of waking; take a 5-minute light walk or stretch | Reduce dehydration-related fatigue and morning stiffness |
| Daily work blocks | Eye strain control | Use the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look 20 feet away for 20 seconds; blink fully 10 times after each break | Ease eye fatigue and screen-related headaches |
| Daily lunch | Midday reset | Eat lunch away from the screen; add water or unsweetened tea; step outside for 5–10 minutes if possible | Break up visual load and support hydration |
| Daily 2–4 PM | Headache prevention window | Set a reminder for water, posture check, and a 2-minute neck/shoulder stretch; dim screen brightness slightly if needed | Prevent the common afternoon dip |
| Daily evening | Sleep wind-down | Stop caffeine by early afternoon; reduce bright screens 60 minutes before bed; keep bedtime consistent | Improve sleep quality and next-day energy |
| Mon/Wed/Fri | Allergy support | Use saline nasal rinse or saline spray after outdoor exposure; shower or wash face before bed on high-pollen days | Reduce pollen carryover and congestion |
| Tue/Thu | Movement break | Do a 15–20 minute walk or light exercise after work | Support circulation, stress relief, and sleep |
| Sat | Reset day | Clean glasses/screens, refill water bottle, review headache triggers, restock any OTC items | Keep the routine easy to maintain |
| Sun | Planning day | Prep work snacks, set reminders, and choose 2–3 “must-do” habits for the week | Make the week more realistic |

## Budget-Friendly Support Plan

| Item | Typical Use | Approx. Monthly Cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Electrolyte packets or low-sugar mix | 1 serving on long or sweaty days | USD 8–15 | Helpful if plain water intake is inconsistent |
| Artificial tears, preservative-free | As needed for dry eyes | USD 10–20 | Useful for screen dryness; ask about compatible options |
| Saline nasal spray or rinse | During allergy days | USD 6–15 | Non-medicated and generally low-risk |
| Magnesium glycinate or citrate | Evening, if appropriate | USD 10–20 | Can help some people with sleep or headaches, but check for interactions and GI tolerance |
| Blue-light filtering glasses or screen filter | Work hours | One-time purchase, not monthly | Optional; often less important than breaks and brightness control |

## What to Discuss With a Pharmacist or Doctor

- Whether your headache pattern sounds more like eye strain, dehydration, tension-type headache, migraine, or allergy-related pressure
- If preservative-free artificial tears are a good fit for your screen use and dry-eye symptoms
- Whether a magnesium supplement is appropriate for you, and what form/dose is safest
- If your seasonal allergies would benefit from an OTC antihistamine or nasal steroid, especially if congestion affects sleep
- Whether any supplement could interact with medicines, caffeine use, reflux, kidney issues, or stomach sensitivity
- What warning signs would mean you should get checked sooner, such as worsening headaches, vision changes, one-sided pain, fever, or headaches that wake you from sleep

# 2018 Toyota Corolla: Likely Causes and First Checks

Your symptoms point to a few common, fixable issues: **wheel/tire imbalance or tire wear**, **brake pad/rotor or brake hardware wear**, and possibly **a dragging brake or alignment issue** contributing to the fuel-economy drop. With a **USD 700 budget**, the best approach is to inspect the low-cost, high-probability items first.

## Troubleshooting Checklist and Most Likely Issues

| Step | What to Inspect | Why It Matters | Likelihood |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Tire pressure, tread wear, bulges, and embedded debris | Uneven or damaged tires can cause highway vibration and reduce MPG | High |
| 2 | Wheel balance and wheel condition | A slight highway-speed vibration is classic wheel imbalance or a bent wheel | High |
| 3 | Brake pad thickness and rotor condition | Light squeaking during gentle braking often comes from worn pads or glazed rotors | High |
| 4 | Brake drag after a drive | A sticking caliper or slide pin can cause squeak, heat, and MPG loss | Medium-High |
| 5 | Alignment and suspension play | Misalignment or worn suspension parts can add vibration and hurt fuel economy | Medium |
| 6 | Engine air filter, spark plugs, and basic engine scan | Less likely for the vibration, but can contribute to MPG loss | Medium |
| 7 | Wheel bearings and CV joints | Usually more noise than squeak, but worth checking if vibration persists | Medium-Low |

## What Is Most Likely

### 1) Tire or wheel issue
- **Most likely cause of the highway vibration**
- Common possibilities:
  - Wheel weights lost
  - Tire out of balance
  - Tire wear pattern like cupping
  - Slightly bent wheel
  - Tire pressure off on one or more tires

### 2) Brake wear or brake hardware issue
- **Most likely cause of the light squeaking**
- Common possibilities:
  - Pads near wear limit
  - Glazed pads or rotors
  - Missing or worn anti-rattle clips
  - Dust shield lightly rubbing
- If the squeak happens mostly at low-speed or light pedal pressure, brakes move higher on the list.

### 3) Dragging brake
- This can explain **both the MPG drop and a brake-related sound**
- Signs:
  - One wheel feels much hotter than the others after driving
  - Car feels slightly held back
  - Burning smell near one wheel
- A stuck caliper slide pin or caliper piston is a common repair.

### 4) Alignment or suspension wear
- Can worsen highway vibration and fuel economy
- More likely if:
  - Steering wheel is off-center
  - Car pulls to one side
  - Tires show uneven edge wear

## First Things to Inspect at Home

### Quick visual checks
- Check all four tire pressures when cold and set them to the door-jamb sticker.
- Look for uneven tire wear, bulges, bubbles, or a missing wheel weight.
- Inspect whether one tire has a different tread pattern or is more worn than the others.
- Look through the wheel spokes for brake dust buildup or a rotor with heavy scoring.

### Simple brake checks
- After a normal drive, carefully compare wheel temperatures:
  - One wheel much hotter than the others suggests brake drag.
- In a quiet area, test whether squeak happens:
  - Only when braking lightly
  - Only at low speed
  - Also when not braking
- If the noise changes when you gently apply more pedal pressure, pads/rotors are more likely than suspension.

### Simple vibration checks
- Note the speed range:
  - If vibration starts around **55–75 mph**, wheel/tire balance is especially likely.
- See whether vibration is:
  - In the steering wheel = front tires/wheels
  - In the seat/floor = rear tires/wheels or driveline-related
- If the vibration changes when you slightly turn left or right, tire or wheel issues are even more likely.

## Best Order to Spend Your Budget

| Priority | Service/Check | Typical Cost Range | Expected Value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Tire inspection + balance | USD 60–150 | Often fixes highway vibration quickly |
| 2 | Brake inspection + pad/rotor measurement | USD 0–100 inspection, more if repaired | Best way to confirm squeak source |
| 3 | Alignment check | USD 100–150 | Helps MPG and tire wear if out of spec |
| 4 | Brake service for stuck slide pins/caliper | USD 150–400 | Important if one wheel is dragging |
| 5 | Air filter, spark plugs, basic engine scan | USD 80–250 depending on parts/labor | Useful if MPG drop remains after tire/brake fixes |

## What to Tell the Mechanic

Use this short description:
- Slight vibration at highway speeds for 2 weeks
- Light squeak during gentle braking
- Fuel economy down about 10%
- Mostly city driving
- Budget about USD 700
- Please check tires, wheel balance, brake wear, and whether any brake is dragging

## Best First Move

If you want the highest chance of solving this cheaply, start with:
1. **Tire pressure and tread inspection**
2. **Wheel balance check**
3. **Brake inspection for pad wear, rotor glazing, and stuck caliper pins**
4. **Alignment check if tires or steering wheel show uneven wear or pull**

# Likely Causes of a 9-Day Dry Cough

Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/cup-hot.svg

Given your age, generally good health, no fever, and a dry cough with mild fatigue and scratchy throat, the most likely non-emergency causes are:
- **Viral upper respiratory infection**: a common cold or post-viral cough can linger for 1–3 weeks.
- **Post-nasal drip from allergies**: especially if you already take **cetirizine** and still have throat irritation or throat-clearing.
- **Mild throat irritation**: from dry air, mouth breathing, smoke, dust, or frequent coughing.
- **COVID-19 or another respiratory virus**: can present without fever and with fatigue, sore/scratchy throat, and dry cough.
- **Acid reflux / silent reflux**: can cause a dry cough and scratchy throat, often worse after meals or when lying down.

# Self-Care and When to Get Checked

## What to do over the next few days
- **Hydrate well**: warm fluids can help soothe the throat.
- **Honey**: 1–2 teaspoons as needed can reduce cough; avoid in children under 1 year, but it is fine for adults.
- **Throat lozenges or hard candies**: help with scratchiness and cough triggers.
- **Humidifier or steamy shower**: useful if dry air is making symptoms worse.
- **Avoid irritants**: smoke, vaping, strong fragrances, dust, and very cold air.
- **Sleep with your head slightly elevated**: helpful if post-nasal drip or reflux is contributing.
- **Continue cetirizine as directed** if it helps your allergies; if your nose is congested or dripping, an allergy/post-nasal drip pattern is more likely.
- **Consider a COVID test** if you have exposure, are around vulnerable people, or want to rule it out.

## Red flags that should prompt medical care
Seek urgent care sooner if you develop:
- **Shortness of breath**
- **Chest pain**
- **Wheezing that is new or significant**
- **Fever that starts later, or fever over 100.4°F / 38°C**
- **Coughing up blood**
- **Blue lips, severe weakness, confusion, or fainting**
- **Signs of dehydration**: very dark urine, dizziness, inability to keep fluids down
- **A rapidly worsening cough** or trouble speaking in full sentences

## When to arrange a routine visit
Make a non-urgent appointment if:
- The cough lasts **more than 3 weeks**
- Symptoms are **not improving after 10–14 days**
- You have **recurrent episodes** of cough
- You notice **heartburn, sour taste, or cough that is worse at night**
- You have **persistent fatigue** or new symptoms that are not typical for a simple cold

## 72-hour symptom-tracking plan
Track the same 5 items morning and evening:
- **Cough frequency**: none / mild / moderate / frequent
- **Energy level**: 0–10
- **Throat irritation**: 0–10
- **Nasal symptoms**: none / drip / congestion / sneezing
- **Triggers**: meals, lying down, talking, exercise, cold air, dust, smoke

### Simple check-in schedule
- **Now**: note current cough severity, throat scratchiness, and any triggers from the last few hours.
- **24 hours**: compare whether cough is better, worse, or unchanged after hydration, honey, and humidified air.
- **48 hours**: look for a pattern suggesting allergy/post-nasal drip, reflux, or a viral illness.
- **72 hours**: if there is no improvement, or if symptoms are worsening, arrange medical evaluation.

## Quick interpretation guide
- **More sneezing, runny nose, or throat-clearing** → more consistent with **allergy/post-nasal drip**
- **Worse after meals or when lying down** → more consistent with **reflux**
- **Body aches, exposure to a sick contact, or gradual improvement over days** → more consistent with a **viral illness**
- **New breathing symptoms or fever** → needs **medical review**

# London Deposit Dispute: Evidence and Next Steps

A calm, well-documented approach usually gives you the best chance of getting the deposit back without turning it into a long conflict. In the UK, the key is to show the property condition at move-in vs move-out and keep all communication professional.

## What to Gather Before Replying

- **Move-in photos/videos** showing walls, carpet, skirting boards, and any pre-existing marks
- **Move-out photos/videos** taken on or around 2026-02-28, ideally with timestamps
- **Inventory/check-in report** and any signed condition notes
- **Check-out report** if the landlord or agent produced one
- **Email trail** with dates, promises, complaints, repair requests, and any acknowledgments
- **Tenancy agreement** and any clause about wear and tear, cleaning, or redecorating
- **Deposit protection details**: scheme name, deposit amount, and reference number
- **Repair history**: messages about leaks, damp, stains, or prior wall/carpet issues
- **Witness notes** from anyone who saw the property at move-in or move-out
- **Receipts** for professional cleaning, carpet cleaning, or repairs if you paid for them
- **A simple timeline** of events: move-in, issues reported, move-out, landlord claim, your response

## Practical Checklist for Your Dispute

- Compare each alleged issue against move-in evidence side by side
- Separate **fair wear and tear** from actual damage
- Note whether the carpet was already old, worn, stained, or discoloured
- Check whether wall marks are minor scuffs, nail holes, or something more serious
- Ask for itemised evidence of the landlord’s claim and repair quotes
- Keep copies of everything in one folder, with file names by date
- Save emails as PDFs or screenshots in case messages are deleted
- Avoid admitting liability before seeing the landlord’s evidence
- Keep your tone factual, polite, and short
- If the landlord claims costs, ask how they were calculated and whether depreciation was applied
- If the deposit is protected, use the scheme’s dispute process if needed

## Calm Dispute Email Template

Subject: Deposit return request and evidence review

Hello [Landlord/Agent Name],

I hope you are well. I am writing about the deposit for [property address], following the end of my tenancy on 2026-02-28.

I do not agree that the deposit should be withheld for the alleged wall and carpet damage. My move-in and move-out photos, together with the email trail, show the condition of the property and help distinguish any pre-existing issues and normal wear and tear from anything that may be disputed.

Please could you send:
- A clear list of the items you believe should be deducted
- The specific photos or reports you are relying on
- Any invoices, estimates, or receipts for the proposed work
- An explanation of how you have taken age and fair wear and tear into account

I would like to resolve this amicably and without unnecessary escalation. Once I have reviewed your evidence, I am happy to discuss the matter promptly.

Kind regards,
[Your full name]
[Your phone number]
[Your forwarding address]

## Step-by-Step Resolution Path

1. **Organise your evidence**
   - Put move-in and move-out photos into dated folders
   - Match each disputed item to a photo and note the condition

2. **Reply calmly in writing**
   - Ask for itemised deductions and supporting evidence
   - Do not argue point-by-point until you have their evidence

3. **Check the deposit scheme**
   - Confirm which tenancy deposit protection scheme holds the money
   - Review the scheme’s dispute process and deadlines

4. **Make a reasoned counterproposal**
   - If some deduction seems fair, consider offering a small amount
   - If the claim is inflated, explain why with photos and dates

5. **Use the free dispute service if needed**
   - If you cannot agree, ask the deposit scheme to adjudicate
   - Submit your evidence clearly and keep your timeline concise

6. **Keep the tone neutral**
   - Avoid threats or emotional language
   - Focus on facts, condition, and fairness

7. **Escalate only if necessary**
   - If the landlord refuses to engage or the scheme outcome is unclear, consider advice from a tenant support organisation or a solicitor

## Brake Noise and Steering Vibration Priorities for Your 2017 Corolla

Your symptoms point most strongly to **front brake wear or brake hardware issues**, with a second possibility of **rotor wear/warping** and a separate front-end issue if the highway-speed vibration is not brake-related. Since you want to stay under **$700**, the best approach is to inspect the **front brakes first**, then confirm whether the vibration is from the brakes or from tires/suspension.

## Most Likely Causes and What to Check First

| Priority | Likely cause | Why it fits | What to inspect first | Cost pressure |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Worn front brake pads** | Squealing + longer stopping distance are classic pad-wear signs | Pad thickness, wear indicators, pad glazing | Usually moderate |
| 2 | **Front rotors worn or uneven** | Can cause vibration and reduced braking smoothness | Rotor thickness, scoring, runout, hot spots | Can push cost up |
| 3 | **Sticking caliper or slide pins** | Uneven wear can create noise, pull, and longer stops | Caliper movement, slide pin lubrication, pad wear side-to-side | Often fixable without full replacement |
| 4 | **Brake hardware/shims missing or worn** | Squeal can come from hardware, not just pads | Anti-rattle clips, shims, pad fitment | Lower-cost repair |
| 5 | **Tires or wheel balance** | Highway steering-wheel vibration may be separate from braking | Tire balance, uneven wear, bent wheel, tire pressure | Often cheaper than brake work |
| 6 | **Front suspension/steering wear** | Less likely, but can cause highway vibration | Tie rods, control arm bushings, ball joints | Can exceed budget if major |

### What should be inspected first
1. **Front brake pad thickness**
   - If pads are near minimum, replace them now.
   - Ask whether the inner and outer pads are wearing evenly.

2. **Front rotors**
   - Check for scoring, thickness variation, and runout.
   - If rotors are still within spec, resurfacing may be possible, but many shops prefer replacement.

3. **Calipers and slide pins**
   - A sticking slide pin can make one pad wear faster and create noise.
   - This is important if one wheel is hotter or more worn than the other.

4. **Brake hardware**
   - Missing or worn shims/clips can cause squealing even if pads are not fully worn.

5. **Tires/wheels for the highway vibration**
   - Because the vibration is at highway speeds, ask for a tire balance check and inspection for uneven wear or a bent wheel.
   - If vibration happens mostly while braking, that points more toward rotors than tires.

## Best Repair Path to Stay Under $700

- **Most budget-friendly likely fix:** front pads + hardware service + brake inspection
- **If rotors are needed too:** front pads + rotors + labor may still fit under budget at many independent shops
- **If calipers are sticking:** budget may rise, so confirm that before authorizing rotor replacement
- **If vibration is from tires:** balancing or tire replacement may be a better-value fix than brake work

### Cost-control strategy
- Ask for a **diagnosis first**, not a parts swap.
- Request they measure:
  - pad thickness
  - rotor thickness
  - rotor runout
  - caliper slide movement
  - tire balance and tread wear
- Ask for the **minimum safe repair** that restores braking and stops the squeal.

## Questions to Ask the Mechanic

- “How much pad material is left on the front and rear brakes?”
- “Are the rotors within spec, or are they causing the vibration?”
- “Is the squeal from pad wear indicators, glazed pads, or missing hardware?”
- “Are the caliper slide pins moving freely on both sides?”
- “Do you see uneven pad wear that suggests a sticking caliper?”
- “Is the highway vibration from the brakes, or should we check tire balance and wheel runout?”
- “What is the safest repair that keeps this under $700?”
- “Can you show me the worn parts before replacing anything?”

## 5-Dinner Austin Meal Plan on a USD 85 Budget
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/cup-hot.svg

Built for 2 adults, high protein, no shellfish, one vegetarian dinner, and under 35 minutes per meal. I’ve kept ingredients overlapping across the week to cut waste and stay close to a typical Austin grocery budget.

## Dinner Lineup and Grocery Overlap
| Dinner | Main Protein | Time | Why It Fits |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Turkey taco rice bowls | Ground turkey | 25 min | Fast, high-protein, uses rice, beans, onion, peppers |
| Sheet-pan chicken fajitas | Chicken thighs | 30 min | Shared fajita veggies, tortillas, salsa, yogurt |
| Turkey marinara pasta | Ground turkey | 30 min | Uses onion, garlic, pasta, canned tomatoes |
| Black bean and egg breakfast tacos | Eggs + black beans | 20 min | Vegetarian, cheap, filling, uses tortillas and salsa |
| Lemon-garlic chicken and broccoli bowls | Chicken thighs | 30 min | Reuses rice, broccoli, garlic, lemon, yogurt |

### Meal 1: Turkey Taco Rice Bowls
- Brown **1 lb ground turkey** with onion, garlic, chili powder, cumin, salt, and pepper.
- Stir in **1 can black beans** and a little salsa; warm through.
- Serve over rice with shredded lettuce, diced tomato, and a spoon of yogurt or sour cream.

### Meal 2: Sheet-Pan Chicken Fajitas
- Toss sliced chicken thighs, bell peppers, and onion with oil, chili powder, cumin, paprika, salt, and pepper.
- Roast at **425°F for 20–25 minutes** until chicken is cooked through.
- Serve in tortillas with salsa and yogurt.

### Meal 3: Turkey Marinara Pasta
- Cook pasta while browning **1 lb ground turkey** with onion and garlic.
- Add marinara sauce and a splash of water; simmer 5–8 minutes.
- Toss with pasta and top with a little cheese if desired.

### Meal 4: Black Bean and Egg Breakfast Tacos
- Warm black beans in a pan with cumin, salt, and a little salsa.
- Scramble eggs and fold in spinach or peppers if you have them.
- Fill tortillas with beans, eggs, and salsa.

### Meal 5: Lemon-Garlic Chicken and Broccoli Bowls
- Cook rice if needed.
- Sauté chicken thighs with garlic, lemon juice, salt, pepper, and a little oil.
- Add broccoli and a splash of water; cover until tender-crisp, then serve over rice with yogurt on the side.

# Mortgage Choice for an 8-Year Dublin Homebuyer

For a first-time buyer in Dublin planning to stay **8+ years**, with a **15% deposit**, a **€1,900 monthly cap**, and a clear preference for **lower risk**, a **fixed-rate mortgage** is usually the stronger fit. A variable rate can start cheaper, but it exposes you to payment rises that matter more over an 8-year holding period.

## Fixed vs Variable: What Matters Most

| Factor | Fixed-rate mortgage | Variable-rate mortgage |
|---|---|---|
| Monthly payment | Predictable for the fixed term | Can rise or fall over time |
| Risk level | Lower | Higher |
| Best for | Buyers who want certainty and budgeting stability | Buyers who can handle payment swings |
| Early years | Often slightly higher starting rate | Often lower initial rate |
| 8-year stay | Usually easier to plan around | More exposed to rate changes across the period |
| Budget fit at €1,900 cap | Easier to stress-test and control | May fit now, but less secure if rates climb |

## Which Is Better for This Buyer?

**Recommended direction: fixed-rate mortgage.**

Why it fits your situation:
- You plan to stay **at least 8 years**, so payment stability matters more than chasing the cheapest first year.
- Your priority is **lower risk**, and fixed rates protect you from surprise increases.
- With a **15% deposit**, keeping the monthly payment predictable helps reduce strain if other costs rise.
- A monthly ceiling of **€1,900** suggests you should favor certainty over short-term savings.

### Practical rule of thumb
- Choose **fixed** if you want to know exactly what your mortgage payment will be for the next few years.
- Choose **variable** only if you are comfortable with the payment changing and you have room in your budget for increases.

## Simple Decision Checklist

- [ ] Do I want my payment to stay predictable for budgeting?
- [ ] Would a rise in interest rates make my monthly budget tight?
- [ ] Am I planning to keep the home for more than 5 years?
- [ ] Do I prefer safety over the chance of a slightly lower initial rate?
- [ ] Could I still afford payments if rates moved up?

**If you answered “yes” to most of these, fixed-rate is the better match.**

## Common Mistakes to Avoid

- **Choosing the lowest initial rate without checking future risk**
  - A variable rate may look cheaper at first but can become more expensive later.

- **Ignoring the full cost over 8 years**
  - Focus on the likely long-term cost, not just the first monthly payment.

- **Not stress-testing the budget**
  - Make sure you could still manage if rates increase or other household costs rise.

- **Assuming you will refinance easily later**
  - Future income, rates, and lending rules may not cooperate.

- **Overstretching just because the lender approves it**
  - Approval does not always mean comfortable affordability.

## Allergy-Related Symptom Snapshot
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/cloud-sun.svg
A 34-year-old with seasonal allergies, **3 days** of mild sore throat, runny nose, and low energy, **no fever**, already taking **cetirizine daily**.
This pattern often fits a mild viral upper-respiratory irritation or allergy flare, but it should be watched for worsening or red-flag symptoms.

## Self-Care Checklist for the Next 48–72 Hours
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/thermometer-half.svg
- **Hydration:** Aim for frequent sips of water, warm tea, broth, or electrolyte drinks if appetite is low.
- **Rest:** Prioritize sleep and reduce intense exercise until energy improves.
- **Throat comfort:** Use warm salt-water gargles, lozenges, honey in warm water/tea if desired.
- **Nasal care:** Consider saline spray or rinse to ease congestion and post-nasal drip.
- **Allergy control:** Keep taking cetirizine as directed; reduce pollen exposure when possible.
- **Food:** Choose light, easy-to-tolerate meals; avoid alcohol and smoking/vaping, which can irritate the throat.
- **Monitoring:** Check for fever, worsening throat pain, shortness of breath, or symptoms lasting beyond about a week.

## When to Seek Medical Care
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/phone.svg
Urgent evaluation is warranted if any of these occur:
- Trouble breathing, wheezing, chest pain, or blue lips
- Swelling of the tongue, lips, face, or throat
- Severe throat pain with drooling, muffled voice, or inability to swallow liquids
- High fever, stiff neck, confusion, or severe weakness
- Signs of dehydration: very dark urine, dizziness, fainting, inability to keep fluids down
- Symptoms that rapidly worsen, or a new rash/hives with breathing symptoms
- One-sided throat swelling, severe ear pain, or pus on the tonsils
- Symptoms lasting more than 7–10 days, or improving then suddenly getting worse

## What This Most Likely Means
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/clipboard-heart.svg
- **Most likely:** mild viral illness, allergy irritation, or both
- **Less concerning if:** symptoms stay mild, no fever develops, and breathing/swallowing remain normal
- **Get checked sooner if:** you have known strep exposure, significant throat pain, or symptoms are not trending better

# Likely Causes of Your Sore Throat, Congestion, and Night Cough

Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/thermometer-half.svg

Given **5 days** of sore throat, congestion, and a cough that’s worse at night, with **no fever**, the most likely non-emergency causes are:
- **Viral upper respiratory infection** — a common cold can cause sore throat, stuffiness, and cough for 1–2 weeks.
- **Postnasal drip** from a cold or allergies — mucus draining down the throat often causes a **night cough** and throat irritation.
- **Allergic rhinitis / seasonal allergies** — especially if you also have sneezing, itchy eyes, or symptoms that fluctuate with exposure.
- **Mild asthma irritation** — congestion and postnasal drip can make cough and nighttime chest tightness worse, even without a full asthma flare.

# Most Helpful Self-Care and OTC Options

Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/cup-hot.svg

A practical plan is to reduce throat irritation, thin mucus, and keep your airways calm.

- **Hydration and humidified air**
  - Drink fluids regularly.
  - Use a cool-mist humidifier at night if your room is dry.
  - Warm tea or broth can soothe throat irritation.

- **Salt-water gargles**
  - Gargle with warm salt water 3–4 times daily for throat pain.

- **Honey for cough**
  - 1–2 teaspoons before bed can help nighttime cough.
  - Do not use honey for children under 1 year, but that does not apply to you.

- **Nasal saline**
  - Saline spray or rinse can reduce postnasal drip and congestion.
  - This is one of the safest options and often helps cough that’s worse at night.

- **Sleep positioning**
  - Raise your head slightly with an extra pillow.
  - This can reduce drainage and nighttime coughing.

### OTC options that may help
- **Cetirizine**: continue if it helps your allergies.
- **Intranasal steroid spray** such as **fluticasone** or **triamcinolone**:
  - Often very helpful for congestion, postnasal drip, and allergy-related symptoms.
  - Works best when used daily for several days, not just once.
- **Decongestants**:
  - **Pseudoephedrine** can help congestion but may raise heart rate, cause jitteriness, or worsen insomnia.
  - **Oxymetazoline nasal spray** can work quickly, but use for **no more than 3 days** to avoid rebound congestion.
- **Pain/fever relief if needed**:
  - **Acetaminophen** or **ibuprofen** can help sore throat discomfort.
- **Cough suppressants**:
  - **Dextromethorphan** may help if the cough is keeping you awake.
  - If mucus is thick, **guaifenesin** may help loosen it, especially with good hydration.

### Asthma-specific note
Because you have mild asthma, pay attention to whether this cough feels like:
- wheezing,
- chest tightness,
- shortness of breath,
- or needing albuterol more often than usual.

If so, the cough may be partly asthma-related, not just from throat irritation.

# When to Seek Clinician Care

Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/phone.svg

You should arrange medical evaluation if any of these happen:
- Symptoms last **more than 10 days** without improvement.
- You get **fever**, or symptoms suddenly worsen after starting to improve.
- You have **shortness of breath, wheezing, chest tightness, or trouble speaking full sentences**.
- Your **albuterol** is needed more often than usual or is not helping.
- You develop **severe sore throat**, trouble swallowing, drooling, or muffled voice.
- You notice **one-sided sinus pain**, facial swelling, or thick nasal drainage that persists.
- You have **chest pain**, coughing up blood, or severe fatigue.
- You have repeated nighttime coughing that is persistent enough to suggest an asthma flare or another treatable cause.
- You are unsure whether this is a cold, allergies, sinus infection, or asthma worsening.

### Urgent care or emergency signs
Seek urgent help now if you have:
- significant breathing trouble,
- blue lips,
- severe wheezing,
- confusion,
- or symptoms that are rapidly worsening.

# What This Most Likely Means for You

Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/cloud-sun.svg

Most likely, this is **a viral cold, allergies, or postnasal drip**, with your **night cough possibly amplified by mild asthma**. A good first approach is:
- continue cetirizine,
- add saline rinses,
- consider a daily nasal steroid spray,
- use honey at night,
- and monitor whether albuterol use increases.

# 8-Week SQL Learning Plan for Business Data Analysis

A hands-on plan built for **5 hours per week**. It focuses on practical querying skills first, then moves into joins, aggregations, and window functions so you can analyze business data confidently.

## Weekly Roadmap

| Week | Focus | Practice Tasks | Goal |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | SQL basics and SELECT | Query a sample table; filter rows with WHERE; sort results; limit output | Read and shape data from one table |
| 2 | Data types and logic | Use AND/OR/NOT; work with NULL; format dates/text; practice CASE statements | Write cleaner, more useful filters |
| 3 | Aggregations | Use COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX; group data with GROUP BY; filter groups with HAVING | Summarize business metrics |
| 4 | Joins I | Practice INNER, LEFT, and FULL joins; match keys across tables; identify missing matches | Combine data from multiple tables |
| 5 | Joins II and data modeling basics | Work with one-to-many relationships; avoid duplicate counts; build join chains | Handle realistic business datasets |
| 6 | Window functions | Use ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK; running totals; moving averages; partition by groups | Compare rows without collapsing detail |
| 7 | Analysis patterns | Cohort-style analysis; top customers/products; monthly trends; segmentation with CASE | Answer common business questions |
| 8 | Mini-project and review | Build a full analysis from raw tables to insights; rewrite queries for clarity; document findings | Produce a portfolio-ready SQL analysis |

## Weekly Practice Plan

### Week 1: SQL Basics
- Learn: `SELECT`, `FROM`, `WHERE`, `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT`
- Practice:
  - Pull 10 rows from a sales table
  - Filter orders by region, status, or date
  - Sort by revenue descending
- Hands-on goal: answer “What happened?” from one table

### Week 2: Logic, NULLs, and CASE
- Learn: comparison operators, boolean logic, `IS NULL`, `CASE`
- Practice:
  - Find missing values in customer or order data
  - Create labels like `new`, `repeat`, `high value`
  - Bucket order amounts into ranges
- Hands-on goal: turn raw data into usable categories

### Week 3: Aggregations
- Learn: `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `GROUP BY`, `HAVING`
- Practice:
  - Total sales by month
  - Average order value by region
  - Top 10 products by revenue
  - Filter groups with fewer than 5 orders
- Hands-on goal: summarize performance clearly

### Week 4: Joins I
- Learn: `INNER JOIN`, `LEFT JOIN`, `FULL OUTER JOIN`
- Practice:
  - Join orders to customers
  - Join order items to products
  - Find customers with no orders
- Hands-on goal: combine related tables without losing meaning

### Week 5: Joins II and Common Pitfalls
- Learn: one-to-many joins, join keys, duplicate rows, grain of data
- Practice:
  - Count unique customers correctly after joins
  - Compare order-level vs item-level analysis
  - Trace why totals change after a join
- Hands-on goal: avoid inflated counts and broken metrics

### Week 6: Window Functions
- Learn: `OVER`, `PARTITION BY`, `ORDER BY`, `ROW_NUMBER`, `RANK`, running totals
- Practice:
  - Rank customers by revenue within each region
  - Calculate cumulative monthly sales
  - Find each customer’s first order
- Hands-on goal: analyze trends and rankings without grouping away detail

### Week 7: Business Analysis Patterns
- Learn: common reporting patterns used in BI and analytics
- Practice:
  - Monthly revenue trend
  - Repeat purchase rate
  - Top customers by segment
  - Product performance by category
- Hands-on goal: answer business questions end-to-end

### Week 8: Mini-Project and Review
- Learn: query organization, naming, simple documentation
- Practice:
  - Build a full analysis from question to insight
  - Re-run and refine earlier queries
  - Write a short summary of findings
- Hands-on goal: create a complete analysis you can show or reuse

## Mini-Project Idea: Business Sales Performance Report

## 2-Week Sleep Improvement Plan

You’re starting from a solid baseline: regular exercise, no major health red flags, and a clear target of improving sleep quality without medication. The main levers here are **earlier caffeine cutoff, more consistent sleep timing, and a short wind-down routine**.

## 14-Day Sleep Reset Plan

| Week | Focus | Habit Changes | Bedtime Routine | Tracking Goal |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Days 1-3 | Stabilize the schedule | Keep wake time within 30 minutes daily; avoid naps after 3 PM; keep coffee only before 14:00 | 20 min: dim lights, wash up, set clothes/tasks for tomorrow | Record bedtime, wake time, caffeine cutoff |
| Days 4-7 | Improve wind-down | Move last coffee to 13:00-14:00; finish exercise at least 3 hours before bed; reduce bright screens 45 min before sleep | 25 min: shower, light stretch, read 10 min, lights out | Rate sleep quality 1-5 each morning |
| Days 8-10 | Increase sleep opportunity | Shift bedtime 15-30 min earlier if you’re still sleepy in the morning; keep weekends within 1 hour of weekday wake time | 30 min: no work email, no heavy news, calm breathing for 5 min | Track time to fall asleep and night awakenings |
| Days 11-14 | Lock in what works | Keep caffeine cutoff at 13:00 if possible; protect a consistent wake time; avoid alcohol close to bedtime if applicable | 30 min: same sequence nightly, same order, same lights-out time | Note energy, focus, and morning alertness |

## Daily Bedtime Routine

### 30-Minute Wind-Down
- **30 min before bed:** dim lights, silence notifications, stop work tasks
- **20 min before bed:** hygiene routine, prepare water, set alarm, lay out tomorrow’s essentials
- **10 min before bed:** light reading, calm music, or slow breathing
- **At lights out:** keep the room cool, dark, and quiet; use the bed only for sleep

### Simple Rules That Matter Most
- Keep **wake time consistent** every day
- Aim for **7.0-7.5 hours in bed** to start, then adjust based on how you feel
- Move caffeine earlier if sleep feels light or delayed
- If you can’t fall asleep after about 20-30 minutes, get up briefly and do something quiet until sleepy

## Tracking Checklist

Use this each day for 14 days.

- [ ] Wake time within 30 minutes of target
- [ ] Caffeine stopped by target cutoff
- [ ] Exercise finished at least 3 hours before bed
- [ ] Screens reduced in the last 45 minutes
- [ ] Bedtime routine completed
- [ ] Lights out at target time
- [ ] Estimated time to fall asleep: ___ minutes
- [ ] Night awakenings: ___
- [ ] Morning sleep quality: 1 2 3 4 5
- [ ] Daytime energy: 1 2 3 4 5

## What to Watch For

- If you feel groggy in the morning, your bedtime may be too late or your sleep may be too fragmented.
- If you lie awake often, caffeine timing and evening screen/light exposure are the first things to tighten.
- If you improve after 2 weeks, keep the habits that gave the biggest boost and make only one change at a time after that.

# Berlin 12-Month Lease Review Checklist

A practical tenant-side guide for a **2-bedroom, 72 m² apartment in Berlin** with **€1,650 rent + €220 utilities** and move-in on **2026-06-01**. Use this to spot common contract issues, prepare questions, and review the lease before signing.

## Lease Clauses to Verify Before You Sign

- **Parties and apartment details**: landlord name, tenant names, full address, unit number, floor, and exact apartment size.
- **Lease term**: confirm it is truly **12 months**, with clear start and end dates.
- **Rent structure**: separate **cold rent** from **utilities/Nebenkosten**; verify what the €220 covers and whether it is a fixed advance or a flat fee.
- **Deposit/Kaution**: amount, payment timing, and whether it is held in a separate protected account.
- **Included furnishings and condition**: check whether the apartment is unfurnished, partly furnished, or includes appliances; attach a signed handover protocol.
- **Heating, water, electricity, internet**: confirm which services are included and which you must contract separately.
- **Maintenance and repairs**: know who handles minor repairs, appliance issues, and emergency fixes.
- **Subletting and guests**: check whether subletting is allowed and what approval is needed.
- **Notice and extension rules**: verify what happens at the end of the 12 months and whether renewal is automatic, optional, or requires notice.
- **House rules**: quiet hours, pets, smoking, waste sorting, laundry use, and bike storage.

## Practical Questions to Ask the Landlord

| Topic | What to ask | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Rent | Is €1,650 the cold rent, and is €220 a fixed utility advance or a true all-in amount? | Prevents surprise monthly costs |
| Utilities | What exactly is included in the €220: heating, water, waste, building costs, internet? | Clarifies monthly budget |
| Deposit | How much is the deposit, when is it due, and how is it protected? | Helps avoid cash-flow and security issues |
| Repairs | Which repairs are the tenant’s responsibility, and is there a repair cap? | Avoids unfair maintenance clauses |
| Handover | Will there be a signed move-in condition report with photos? | Protects you from damage disputes |
| Term end | What happens after 12 months: renewal, extension, or move-out? | Avoids last-minute uncertainty |
| Registration | Can I get the landlord confirmation needed for Berlin registration (Anmeldung)? | Important for settling in |
| Keys/access | How many keys are provided, and are there building/access codes? | Practical move-in readiness |

## Contract Warning Signs to Watch For

- **Unclear rent wording**: if the contract mixes cold rent, utilities, and extra charges without explanation.
- **Open-ended repair duties**: clauses that make you responsible for broad or unlimited repairs.
- **Automatic renewals with short notice**: especially if the notice deadline is unusually strict.
- **Penalty-style fees**: charges for normal wear, standard cleaning, or vague “administration” costs.
- **Deposit terms that are vague**: no clear timing, no separate account, or deductions not tied to documented damage.
- **Restrictive use clauses**: rules that seem to forbid normal living activities without a good reason.
- **Missing handover protocol**: no written inventory, meter readings, or condition notes at move-in.
- **Unclear utility settlement**: no explanation of how annual reconciliation works if utilities are estimated.
- **Oral promises not written in the lease**: if something important was promised, make sure it is added to the contract.

## Move-In Review Checklist

- Confirm the **lease dates** match your move-in plan: **2026-06-01** start date and 12-month end date.
- Verify the **total monthly cost**: **€1,870** before any extra services.
- Read every clause on **deposit, repairs, termination, and utilities**.
- Inspect the apartment and note:
  - walls, floors, windows, bathroom, kitchen, appliances
  - heating function and meter readings
  - keys, mailboxes, cellar/storage, and common areas
- Ask for copies of:
  - signed lease
  - handover protocol
  - energy or utility details if available
  - landlord contact information
- Keep screenshots or copies of all messages and promised terms.

# 2015 Honda Civic: Repair-or-Replace Decision Snapshot

Your Civic is in the **“inspect now, likely repair if the engine/transmission is healthy”** zone. With **128,000 miles**, a **$1,200 repair budget**, and a **50-mile daily commute**, the key question is whether the issue is a **moderate maintenance/ignition/fuel problem** or a **major powertrain repair**.

## Repair vs Replace: Cost-Benefit Comparison

| Option | Upfront Cost | Reliability for 50-mile commute | Best Case | Worst Case |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| Diagnose and repair | **$150–$1,200** | Good if fix is minor | Solves rough idle/MPG drop for months to years | You spend budget and still face bigger repairs soon |
| Repair only if under budget and no major faults | **$0–$1,200** | Fair to good | Keeps car running while you save | Hidden issue returns or escalates |
| Replace the car | **$5,000+ down payment or purchase cost** | Stronger if current car has major problems | Better long-term dependability and fewer surprise repairs | Much higher monthly cost |

## Decision Framework for Your Civic

### Lean toward **repair** if:
- The check engine light points to **spark plugs, coils, oxygen sensor, MAF sensor, vacuum leak, or throttle body cleaning**
- The rough idle is **intermittent** and the car still drives normally
- The repair estimate is **well under $1,200**
- There is **no transmission slip**, overheating, oil burning, or loss of compression

### Lean toward **replace** if:
- The diagnosis shows **engine misfire from compression loss**, **head gasket**, or **catalytic converter damage**
- You get a quote that is **above $1,200** for a repair that does not clearly improve long-term reliability
- The car has **multiple expensive systems failing at once**
- You need maximum certainty for the commute and can’t tolerate another breakdown soon

### Practical rule of thumb
- If the fix is **less than about 20–25% of the car’s likely private-party value**, repairing usually makes sense.
- If the repair is a **major engine or transmission job**, replacement is often smarter.

## Likely Causes for Your Symptoms

| Likely Cause | Why It Fits | Typical Cost Range |
|---|---|---:|
| Worn spark plugs | Can cause rough idle, misfires, worse MPG | **$150–$350** |
| Ignition coil issue | Intermittent rough idle and CEL | **$200–$600** |
| Dirty throttle body / intake carbon | Rough idle, hesitation, MPG drop | **$100–$250** |
| Vacuum leak | Idle instability, lean codes, fuel economy drop | **$120–$500** |
| Oxygen sensor aging | Reduced fuel economy, CEL | **$250–$600** |
| MAF/MAP sensor issue | Bad air/fuel readings, rough running | **$150–$450** |
| Fuel injector issue | Rough idle, misfire, MPG drop | **$200–$900** |
| Catalytic converter efficiency problem | CEL, MPG loss, possible power loss | **$900–$2,500+** |
| Internal engine wear / compression issue | Rough idle, recurring misfires, expensive repair | **$1,500+** |

## Questions to Ask the Mechanic

- What are the **exact OBD-II codes** stored?
- Is the rough idle a **misfire, lean condition, or sensor issue**?
- Which cylinder, if any, is misfiring?
- Are the spark plugs and coils original or recently replaced?
- Is there evidence of a **vacuum leak** or intake air leak?
- Are fuel trims abnormal?
- Is the **fuel economy drop** tied to a sensor, misfire, or mechanical problem?
- Is the engine **burning oil** or losing compression?
- Is the catalytic converter healthy, or is it only reporting a downstream sensor issue?
- What is the **all-in estimate** with parts, labor, tax, and diagnostics?
- What repair would you recommend if this were your own daily driver?

## Best Next Move

### Most likely path
1. Get a **diagnostic scan with codes and freeze-frame data**.
2. Ask for a **tiered estimate**:
   - **Tier 1:** cheapest fix likely to solve it
   - **Tier 2:** best durable fix
   - **Tier 3:** worst-case repair if deeper issues appear
3. Compare the quote to your budget:
   - **Under $500:** usually repair
   - **$500–$1,200:** repair if it addresses the root cause and the car is otherwise sound
   - **Over $1,200:** start seriously considering replacement

### My read for your situation
- A **2015 Civic at 128k** is often still worth repairing if the issue is **ignition, sensors, or intake-related**.
- Because you depend on it daily, you should **prioritize diagnosis quickly** and avoid waiting for the symptom to worsen.
- If the mechanic finds a **major engine or catalytic converter problem**, replacement becomes the stronger financial choice.

# 2-Week Desk-Friendly Wellness Reset

A simple routine can help with sleep, stress, and tension headaches without leaning heavily on supplements. This plan stays allergy-aware, low-cost, and easy to repeat.

## Practical 2-Week Routine

### Daily anchors for both weeks
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/clock.svg
- **Morning:** Get 5–10 minutes of outdoor light within 1 hour of waking.
- **Workday:** Every 50–60 minutes, stand up for 2–3 minutes; do 5 neck rolls, 10 shoulder squeezes, and 10 slow breaths.
- **Hydration:** Aim for regular water intake through the day; use urine color as a rough check.
- **Evening:** Keep caffeine earlier in the day and reduce screens for the last 30–60 minutes before bed.
- **Sleep:** Keep the same wake time daily, even on weekends if possible.

### Week 1: Reset sleep and tension
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/moon-stars.svg
- **Day 1–2:** Set a fixed wake time; move bedtime earlier by 15–30 minutes if you’re currently running short on sleep.
- **Day 1–3:** Add one 10-minute walk after lunch or after work.
- **Day 2–4:** Try a 5-minute wind-down: dim lights, slow breathing, and a short stretch sequence for neck, chest, and upper back.
- **Day 3–5:** Check your desk setup: screen at eye level, shoulders relaxed, feet supported, elbows near 90 degrees.
- **Day 4–7:** If headaches tend to show up, note time, trigger, hydration, sleep, and posture in a quick phone note.

### Week 2: Build consistency and test one optional helper
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/thermometer-half.svg
- **Day 8–10:** Keep the same sleep/wake schedule; add a 10–15 minute walk or light mobility session after work.
- **Day 8–14:** Use a simple evening routine: wash up, prep tomorrow’s clothes/work bag, then 10 minutes of quiet time.
- **Day 9–12:** If allergies are active, use a shower or face rinse after outdoor exposure and keep windows closed on high-pollen days.
- **Day 10–14:** If you want one low-risk product, consider a **HEPA air purifier** for the bedroom or a **simple eye mask/white-noise tool** for sleep.
- **Optional supplement trial:** If you want to test one supplement, choose **one only** for 1–2 weeks so you can tell what helps.

## What to Watch For

### Allergy-safe choices and common cautions
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/shield-check.svg
- **Prefer simple habits first:** sleep timing, light exposure, movement, hydration, and posture usually give the best return.
- **Be cautious with supplements:** “natural” does not always mean safe, especially if you take any medicines.
- **Watch for drowsiness:** some sleep aids, antihistamine-like herbs, or calming supplements can leave you groggy the next day.
- **Watch for headache triggers:** skipped meals, dehydration, jaw clenching, poor monitor position, and long uninterrupted sitting.

## Ranking Framework for Comparing Listings

### Weighted score model
Use a **100-point score** so listings are easy to compare.

- **Commute convenience — 30 points**
  - 30: direct, reliable, short ride to central Manchester
  - 20: one simple change or slightly longer ride
  - 10: workable but slow or unreliable

- **Budget fit — 20 points**
  - 20: comfortably under budget
  - 15: near budget but still manageable
  - 5: over budget or with high extra costs

- **Pet acceptance — 15 points**
  - 15: cat allowed in writing with clear terms
  - 8: pet considered case-by-case
  - 0: no pets

- **Laundry convenience — 15 points**
  - 15: true in-unit washer/dryer
  - 10: in-unit washer only
  - 3: shared laundry
  - 0: none

- **Home quality — 10 points**
  - layout, storage, natural light, noise, heating

- **Lease flexibility — 10 points**
  - move-in date, tenancy length, deposit terms, break clause

### Simple decision rule
- **80+** = strong contender
- **65–79** = worth viewing
- **50–64** = only if trade-offs are acceptable
- **Below 50** = skip unless the price is exceptional

## Trade-Offs to Consider

- **Closer to center vs. more space:** central areas usually improve commute but can reduce size or push rent up.
- **In-unit laundry vs. lower rent:** flats with laundry included often cost more, but save time and hassle.
- **Pet-friendly vs. newer building:** some newer or managed buildings are stricter on pets.
- **Tram access vs. quieter neighborhood:** the best transit locations may be busier or noisier.
- **Short commute vs. better value:** a slightly longer ride can unlock better size, condition, or pet policy.
- **Lower rent vs. higher bills:** older flats may look cheaper but cost more in heating and utilities.
- **Ground floor vs. upper floor:** ground floor can be easier for a cat and moving, but may bring more street noise or security concerns.

## Ontario Freelance Design Setup
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/briefcase.svg

Starting as a sole proprietor in Ontario is straightforward: register only if you need a business name, track income from day one, and use clear client paperwork to protect your time, payment terms, and creative rights.

## Legal Checklist for Freelance Graphic Designers
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/file-earmark-text.svg

- **Choose your business name**
  - If you operate under your own legal name, you may not need a registration.
  - If you use a name like “Studio North Design,” register the business name in Ontario.

- **Register the business name**
  - Search the name first to reduce conflicts.
  - Register through Ontario’s business registry if the name is not your personal legal name.

- **Get a business bank account**
  - Keep business and personal money separate.
  - This makes taxes, bookkeeping, and proof of income much easier.

- **Set up bookkeeping from the start**
  - Save invoices, receipts, contracts, and mileage or home-office records.
  - Track income and expenses monthly, not just at tax time.

- **Check if you need a GST/HST account**
  - You must register once taxable revenue goes over **CAD 30,000** in 4 consecutive calendar quarters.
  - You can register earlier if it helps you claim input tax credits on business expenses.

- **Understand your income tax duty**
  - As a sole proprietor, business profits are reported on your personal tax return.
  - Set aside money regularly for income tax and, if applicable, CPP contributions.

- **Consider insurance**
  - Professional liability and general business insurance can help if a client claims financial loss or there is a dispute.

- **Protect your work**
  - Use written contracts for every client.
  - State clearly who owns the final design files, when ownership transfers, and what rights you keep for portfolio use.

## Client Contract Clauses to Include
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/shield-lock.svg

- **Scope of work**
  - List exactly what you will design, how many concepts/revisions are included, and what is not included.
  - This prevents scope creep.

- **Timeline and milestones**
  - Include start date, review dates, client feedback deadlines, and final delivery date.
  - Say delays caused by late client feedback can shift the schedule.

- **Fees and payment terms**
  - State your rate, deposit amount, when invoices are due, and late-payment charges if allowed.
  - Many freelancers use a non-refundable deposit before starting.

- **Revision limits**
  - Define how many rounds are included.
  - Extra revisions should be billed separately.

- **Intellectual property ownership**
  - Clarify whether you retain copyright until final payment.
  - Specify when the client gets usage rights or full ownership, if that is part of the deal.

- **Portfolio rights**
  - Reserve the right to show finished work in your portfolio unless the client requests confidentiality.
  - If needed, add an approval process for public display.

- **Client responsibilities**
  - Require the client to provide materials, approvals, and legal rights to any logos, photos, text, or fonts they supply.
  - This reduces risk if their content is not cleared for use.

- **Termination**
  - Explain how either side can end the agreement and what gets paid for work already completed.
  - Include what happens to unfinished files.

- **Indemnity and liability limits**
  - Keep this practical and narrow.
  - Limit your responsibility to the amount paid under the contract where appropriate and legally valid.

- **Confidentiality**
  - Use this when you will see private business information, product plans, or unreleased campaigns.

## Tax and Invoicing Basics
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/receipt.svg

- **Invoice each client clearly**
  - Include your legal name or business name, address/contact info, invoice number, date, client name, description of services, amount, and due date.
  - If registered for GST/HST, include your registration number and tax separately.

- **Track deductible expenses**
  - Common examples: software, fonts, stock assets, printing, subcontractors, office supplies, advertising, phone/internet, and a portion of home-office costs if eligible.

- **Save records for at least 6 years**
  - Keep invoices, receipts, bank statements, contracts, and tax filings.

- **Watch for GST/HST charging rules**
  - If you register, you generally must charge GST/HST on taxable services.
  - Make sure your invoices and pricing reflect that.

- **Plan for tax instalments**
  - If your income grows, you may need to make quarterly instalments to the CRA.

## Common Mistakes to Avoid
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/exclamation-triangle.svg

- Working without a written contract
- Starting work before receiving a deposit
- Leaving ownership of files unclear
- Forgetting to define revision limits
- Mixing personal and business spending
- Not registering for GST/HST when required
- Using client-supplied images, fonts, or text without checking rights
- Relying on email messages alone for major deal terms
- Underpricing by failing to account for taxes, admin time, and unpaid revisions
- Not keeping proof of approvals, especially for final files and scope changes

## Practical Starter Workflow
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/check2-circle.svg

- Register your business name if needed
- Open a business bank account
- Create a simple contract template
- Set up an invoice template
- Track income and expenses from the first client
- Review GST/HST registration once revenue starts growing
- Keep a folder for contracts, invoices, receipts, and final deliverables

- Does the system make any **clicking, rattling, or cycling noise** when the AC is on?

- Are there leaks under the engine bay or around the transmission?

# Small Store Sales Dashboard Plan

A simple, manager-friendly dashboard should focus on **daily sales performance, efficiency, and trend direction**. For this 7-day sample, the clearest story is that revenue and orders rise together, while ad spend also climbs and needs efficiency tracking.

## Recommended Dashboard Layout

| Section | What to Show | Best Chart Type | Why It Works |
|---|---|---|---|
| Top KPI strip | Revenue, Orders, Ad Spend, ROAS, AOV | KPI cards | Gives an instant read on business health |
| Sales trend | Orders and Revenue by day | Dual-line chart | Shows whether sales are growing consistently |
| Marketing efficiency | Ad Spend and ROAS by day | Combo chart or line chart | Reveals whether spend is paying off |
| Conversion value | AOV by day | Bar or line chart | Helps spot higher-value order days |
| Daily performance detail | Date, Orders, Revenue, Ad Spend, ROAS, AOV | Compact data table | Useful for quick review and validation |

## Best Chart Types and Metric Priority

### Top of dashboard
Put these metrics in the first row of KPI cards:

- **Revenue**: total sales dollars
- **Orders**: demand volume
- **Ad Spend**: acquisition cost
- **ROAS**: revenue ÷ ad spend
- **AOV**: revenue ÷ orders

### Supporting charts
Use these below the KPI strip:

- **Dual-line chart: Orders vs Revenue**
  - Best for showing growth trend and whether revenue is keeping pace with order volume
- **Line chart or combo chart: Ad Spend vs ROAS**
  - Best for showing whether paid traffic is becoming more efficient
- **Bar chart: AOV by day**
  - Best for identifying higher-value days and basket-size changes
- **Optional table: daily metrics**
  - Best for exact values and manager review

# Roommate Agreement for Two Students in Manchester

A friendly, practical agreement for two students sharing a furnished apartment in Manchester, United Kingdom.
Lease start date: **2026-09-01**

## Roommate Terms and Shared Living Rules

**1) Rent split**
- Total monthly rent will be split **50/50** unless both roommates agree in writing to another split.
- Rent should be paid by each person on or before the same date each month, in line with the lease.
- If one roommate pays the full rent to the landlord or letting agent, the other roommate should transfer their share by the agreed deadline.

**2) Utility split**
- Shared utilities will be split **50/50**, including electricity, gas, water, broadband, and any other agreed household bills.
- If one utility is used only by one roommate, that person should pay the full cost.
- Any bill paid by one roommate on behalf of both should be reimbursed within **7 days** of request or proof of payment.

**3) Cleaning schedule**
- Both roommates agree to keep shared spaces tidy and clean.
- A simple weekly routine will be followed:
  - **Kitchen:** wipe surfaces after use; full clean once per week, alternating responsibility
  - **Bathroom:** quick tidy during the week; deeper clean once per week, alternating responsibility
  - **Living room/common areas:** pick up personal items daily; vacuum or sweep once per week, alternating responsibility
  - **Bins and recycling:** take out when full, alternating as needed
- If one roommate cannot do their turn, they should let the other know in advance and swap tasks or make up the task later.

**4) Guest policy**
- Guests are welcome as long as they are respectful, do not damage property, and do not disturb the other roommate.
- Overnight guests are allowed **occasionally** with reasonable notice.
- No guest should stay for more than **2 consecutive nights** without agreement from both roommates.
- If either roommate is uncomfortable with a guest, that concern should be discussed calmly and respected.

**5) Quiet hours**
- Quiet hours will be from **10:00 PM to 8:00 AM** on weekdays.
- On weekends, quiet hours will be from **11:00 PM to 9:00 AM**.
- During quiet hours, both roommates will keep music, calls, gaming, and other noise low enough not to disturb sleep or study.
- If either roommate has an exam or important deadline, both will try to be extra considerate and agree on any temporary changes.

**6) Shared grocery rules**
- Shared groceries should be agreed in advance, especially for items like milk, bread, rice, cooking oil, and cleaning supplies.
- If an item is bought for both roommates, the cost should be split **50/50** unless agreed otherwise.
- Personal food should be kept separate unless both roommates clearly agree to share it.
- Either roommate should label personal food if needed.
- Shared items should be replaced fairly and without delay when used up.

**7) If one roommate moves out early**
- The roommate who moves out early should give the other roommate as much notice as possible and follow the lease requirements.
- Both roommates will continue to follow the lease until the landlord or letting agent agrees to any change.
- The moving-out roommate remains responsible for their share of rent, utilities, and any damage or unpaid costs up to the end of their responsibility under the lease or replacement agreement.
- If a replacement roommate is allowed, both roommates will cooperate reasonably with the landlord or agent to help arrange it.
- Any deposit issues will be handled according to the tenancy agreement and the landlord’s deposit process.

**8) Respect and communication**
- Both roommates agree to communicate early and respectfully about problems.
- Small issues should be discussed before they become bigger problems.
- Both will try to be fair, flexible, and considerate of each other’s study, sleep, and personal space.

**9) Changes to this agreement**
- Any changes should be agreed by both roommates in writing.
- This agreement is meant to support a calm, friendly home and does not replace the tenancy agreement.

**Signatures**
- Roommate 1: ____________________  Date: ____________________
- Roommate 2: ____________________  Date: ____________________

- Keep a shared note or app for bills, cleaning turns, and grocery purchases.
- Agree early on how rent and utilities will be paid each month.
- Review the agreement after the first month and adjust anything that is not working.

## Introductory Statistics Exam Prep Plan

A focused 5-day plan that prioritizes **hypothesis testing** and **confidence intervals**, then ends with a **mock quiz**. Weekday sessions are set to **2 hours**, and the weekend sessions to **4 hours**.

## 5-Day Study Roadmap

| Day | Time | Daily Topics | Practice Tasks | Revision Strategy |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| Day 1 | 2h | Core concepts; data types; sampling; descriptive statistics | Compute mean, median, mode, variance, and standard deviation from a small dataset; interpret histograms and boxplots | Use a 1-page formula sheet and rewrite key definitions from memory |
| Day 2 | 2h | Probability basics; normal distribution; z-scores; sampling distributions | Solve 8–10 short probability and z-score problems; identify when normal approximation is appropriate | Make quick “if/then” rules for choosing the right method |
| Day 3 | 2h | Confidence intervals; margin of error; interpreting interval results | Build 3 confidence intervals; explain each interval in plain language; check how sample size affects width | Redo one interval without notes, then compare steps with your formula sheet |
| Day 4 | 4h | Hypothesis testing; null vs alternative; p-values; Type I/II errors | Work through 2 full hypothesis tests; practice choosing test direction; interpret p-values and conclusions | Use a decision checklist: state hypotheses, test statistic, p-value, conclusion |
| Day 5 | 4h | Mixed review; weak spots; mock quiz | Complete a timed mock quiz; review every missed question; redo the hardest 5 problems correctly | Finish with an error log: write the mistake, correct method, and takeaway |

## Daily Study Focus

### Day 1: Foundations and Descriptive Statistics
- **Topics:** variables, data types, samples vs populations, central tendency, spread
- **Practice:** calculate summary statistics by hand and with a calculator
- **Goal:** get comfortable with the language of statistics
- **Revision strategy:** create a mini glossary of key terms and test yourself twice

### Day 2: Probability and the Normal Curve
- **Topics:** probability rules, normal distribution, z-scores, sampling distributions
- **Practice:** short calculations and interpretation questions
- **Goal:** improve speed with core probability tools
- **Revision strategy:** draw the normal curve from memory and label key regions

### Day 3: Confidence Intervals
- **Topics:** confidence level, critical values, margin of error, interpretation
- **Practice:** compute intervals and explain what they mean in context
- **Goal:** understand how intervals are built and what they say
- **Revision strategy:** use a 3-step template: identify, calculate, interpret

### Day 4: Hypothesis Testing
- **Topics:** null and alternative hypotheses, test statistic, p-value, significance level, errors
- **Practice:** complete full test problems from start to finish
- **Goal:** become confident in the decision process
- **Revision strategy:** memorize a fixed test sequence and follow it every time

### Day 5: Mixed Review and Mock Quiz
- **Topics:** all major exam areas, with emphasis on weak points
- **Practice:** timed mock quiz plus correction review
- **Goal:** simulate exam conditions and reduce mistakes
- **Revision strategy:** focus only on recurring errors and high-yield formulas

# Phoenix Home Repair Triage for a $500 Budget

A practical plan for a 2,000 sq ft single-family home: fix the highest safety risk first, then the most likely water-damage issue, then the comfort/noise item. With a $500 cap and a preference to avoid unnecessary replacements, the goal is to diagnose before replacing.

## Repair Priority and Likely Approach

| Issue | Priority | Likely DIY vs Pro | Why it matters | Budget range |
|---|---:|---|---|---:|
| Garage door sticks halfway up | 1 | **Professional** | Possible spring/cable/opener issue; can be dangerous | $150–$350+ |
| Leaking kitchen faucet | 2 | **DIY first**, pro if valve/line is damaged | Prevents water waste and cabinet damage | $10–$120 |
| Noisy bathroom exhaust fan | 3 | **DIY first**, pro if motor is failing or wiring is involved | Usually comfort/maintenance, lower urgency | $20–$180 |

## Triage Checklist for the Three Repairs

### 1) Garage Door Sticking Halfway Up
- Do not force the door open or closed.
- Check for visible issues only: loose track hardware, obstructions, frayed cable, or a door that looks uneven.
- If the door feels heavy, jerks, or stops suddenly, stop and call a garage door technician.
- If the opener is the only issue, a simple adjustment or sensor alignment may be enough.
- Avoid spring or cable DIY work; that is the main safety risk.

### 2) Kitchen Faucet Leak
- Determine where the leak is coming from: spout drip, handle base, supply line, or under-sink connection.
- Tighten accessible fittings gently first.
- Replace the cartridge, O-rings, or supply hose only if the leak source is clear.
- Shut off the water before disassembly.
- If the shutoff valve is stuck, corroded, or leaking, use a plumber.

### 3) Bathroom Exhaust Fan Noise
- Clean the grille and fan housing first.
- Check for dust buildup, loose screws, and a rattling cover.
- If the fan blade is accessible, inspect for wobble or debris.
- Replace the fan only if the motor is grinding, humming badly, or intermittently failing.
- If wiring is exposed or the fan is hardwired in a way you are not comfortable with, hire an electrician or handyman.

## Best Order to Handle the Repairs

1. **Garage door**
   - Highest safety concern.
   - Spend money here first only if a pro inspection confirms a real mechanical issue.

2. **Kitchen faucet**
   - Likely the best DIY win.
   - Lowest-cost fix with immediate benefit if it is a simple cartridge, washer, or hose issue.

3. **Bathroom exhaust fan**
   - Address after the leak, unless the fan is sparking, not running at all, or showing electrical symptoms.

## Budget Plan That Fits $500

- Garage door inspection/repair: **$150–$350**
- Faucet parts and supplies: **$20–$80**
- Bathroom fan cleaning/parts: **$20–$100**
- Small reserve for unexpected parts: **$50–$100**

A reasonable target is to keep the garage door under about **$250** if possible, leaving enough room for the faucet and fan without exceeding the cap.

## 6-Week Headache-Reduction Routine

A simple non-medication plan can help if your headaches are mostly tension-type and triggered by sleep debt, screen strain, dehydration, or neck/shoulder tension. The goal is to build a few repeatable habits you can keep on busy weekdays.

## 6-Week Plan for Desk Days

| Week | Focus | Daily routine | Goal |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Baseline + hydration | Track headaches, sleep, screen time, and water; drink regularly through the day | Identify your main triggers |
| 2 | Posture reset | Set up chair/monitor; relax shoulders; do 2-minute neck/shoulder checks 3x/day | Reduce muscle strain |
| 3 | Screen breaks | Use a 20-20-20 eye break and stand/walk briefly every hour | Lower eye and neck fatigue |
| 4 | Sleep upgrade | Move bedtime earlier by 15–30 minutes; keep wake time steady | Add 30–60 minutes of sleep |
| 5 | Stress release | Add 5–10 minutes of breathing or stretching after work | Reduce tension buildup |
| 6 | Review + refine | Compare headache frequency/intensity with week 1; keep what helped most | Make it sustainable |

## Simple Daily Routine

Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/clock.svg

- **Morning:** Drink a full glass of water soon after waking. Eat breakfast if you can, especially on workdays.
- **Before work:** Check desk setup: screen at eye level, feet supported, shoulders relaxed, elbows near your sides.
- **During work:** Every hour, stand up for 1–2 minutes, roll shoulders, and gently stretch neck and upper back.
- **After lunch:** Take a 5-minute walk or do light movement instead of staying seated continuously.
- **Evening:** Reduce bright screens for 30–60 minutes before bed when possible, and keep bedtime/wake time consistent.

## Hydration and Screen-Break Guidance

Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/water.svg

- **Hydration target:** Aim for steady intake across the day rather than large amounts at once.
- **Easy rule:** Drink water at each meal, with each coffee/tea, and after every bathroom break if you tend to forget.
- **Practical check:** Pale yellow urine usually suggests adequate hydration.
- **Screen breaks:** Use the **20-20-20 rule** — every 20 minutes, look 20 feet away for 20 seconds.
- **Movement breaks:** Add a brief standing break at least once per hour; even 1–2 minutes helps.
- **If screens trigger headaches:** Increase font size, reduce glare, and avoid leaning toward the monitor.

## Warning Signs to Get Medical Care

Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/triangle-fill.svg

See a doctor promptly if you have any of these:
- A **sudden, severe “worst headache”** or a headache that peaks very quickly
- **New weakness, numbness, confusion, trouble speaking, fainting, or vision loss**
- **Fever, stiff neck, rash, or severe illness** with the headache
- Headache after **head injury**
- Headaches that are **waking you from sleep**, becoming steadily more frequent, or clearly worsening
- A **new pattern** of headaches after age 30–40, especially if different from your usual headaches
- Headache with **jaw pain when chewing**, scalp tenderness, or other unusual symptoms
- Headaches plus **high blood pressure symptoms** such as chest pain or shortness of breath
- A headache that lasts **more than a few days** or is interfering with work, sleep, or daily function

## Questions for a Primary Care Clinician

Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/phone.svg

- Do these sound more like **tension headaches, migraine, sinus-related pain, or something else**?
- Could my **sleep schedule, desk posture, or screen use** be contributing?
- What **non-medication strategies** do you recommend for prevention?
- Should I keep a **headache diary**, and what details matter most?
- Do I need **vision testing** or a screen/ergonomic evaluation?
- Are my **seasonal allergies** likely playing a role, and how can I reduce that trigger?
- At what point would you want to do **further testing or a referral**?
